The group includes table wine, dessert wine, elderberry wine, fortified and liqueur wines (e.g. port, sherry, vermouth).

entries.label: liqueur or spirits (eurofir)
entries.definition: Alcoholic beverage prepared by fermentation of grain or plant-related products and subsequent distillation. Includes liqueurs (e.g. calvados, kahlua, advocaat) and spirits (e.g. brandy, whisk(e)y, rum).

entries.label: alcoholic mixed drink (eurofir)
entries.definition: Includes cocktails, punch, shandy.

entries.label: miscellaneous food product (eurofir)
entries.definition: EFG group 32, Eurocode-2 group 12.

entries.label: spice, condiment or other ingredient (eurofir)

aliases.norm: spice condiment or other ingredient eurofir

entries.definition: This subgroup includes baking goods and other ingredients such as flavourings, essences, seasonings and extracts which are difficult to assign to other main groups; herbs and spices; dressings, condiments and mixed accompaniments such as chutneys and pickles. The group does not include starches (under *GRAIN OR GRAIN PRODUCT*); plant products that may be used in significant amounts as vegetables a

entries.label: baking ingredient (eurofir)
entries.definition: Includes yeast, baking powder, pectin, additives.

entries.label: flavouring or essence (eurofir)
entries.definition: Includes almond essence, vanilla essence.

entries.label: seasoning or extract (eurofir)
entries.definition: Includes salt, stock cubes, gravy thickener, beef extract, marmite, vinegar.

entries.label: herb or spice (eurofir)
entries.definition: Aromatic or pungent plant product used whole or ground as a seasoning in food products, e.g. basil, oregano, thyme, allspice, clove, paprika, curry powder. Herbs may be considered to be plants whose non-woody parts are consumed in small amounts for their flavouring properties rather than in amounts significant to the intake of major nutrients. Spices are usually a dried part, or parts, of aromatic

entries.label: condiment (eurofir)
entries.definition: Food product that is usually pungent, tart, salty, or spicy and is used to enhance the flavours of other foods; includes ketchup, tabasco sauce, barbeque sauce, vinegar, soy sauce, prepared mustard, prepared horseradish, mint sauce and tartar sauce.

entries.label: dressing, mayonnaise (eurofir)
entries.definition: Mixture of edible fats or oils, acidifying agents and optional ingredients such as sweeteners (nutritive or non-nutritive), starch, egg and seasonings. Used in limited amounts to accompany salads and other foods. Includes salad dressings & other vinegar and oil based cold sauces, mayonnaise & other egg and oil based cold sauces.

entries.label: chutney or pickle (eurofir)
entries.definition: Product prepared by immersing fruits, vegetables, or other ingredients, such as spices and sweeteners, in a brine or an acid solution. Used to enhance the flavour of other food products. Examples are mango chutney, dill pickle, mixed pickle, relish.

entries.label: prepared food product (eurofir)

aliases.text: soup, sauce or miscellaneous food product
aliases.norm: soup sauce or miscellaneous food product

entries.definition: This subgroup includes multicomponent meals, sauces, retail salads, desserts, soups, snacks and other foods where similarity of the product type is more significant than the source of the principal ingredient(s).

entries.label: savoury sauce (eurofir)
entries.definition: Nonstandardized food product used as a meal accompaniment and consisting of a mixture of fats or oils, starch, liquid and other optional ingredients specified by the recipe; excludes condiments. Includes. bolognese sauce , white sauce, brown sauce, butter sauce, tomato sauce.

entries.label: dessert sauce (eurofir)
entries.definition: Sweetened and flavored product that is used as an accompaniment to desserts, e.g. fruit sauce, fudge sauce, brandy sauce.

entries.label: dessert (eurofir)
entries.definition: Sweetened prepared product usually consumed after the main course in a meal. Excludes fruit or fruit products, bakery products and confectionery. Includes sweet puddings (custards, starch puddings), non-dairy ices (e.g. water ices, granitas, sorbets) and gelatine desserts.

entries.label: soup (eurofir)
entries.definition: A liquid food made by simmering meat, poultry, seafood or vegetables, being clear or thickened to the consistency of a thin puree or having milk or cream added, and often containing pieces of solid food such as meat, shellfish, pasta or vegetables. Soup takes precedence over other food products. Examples are egg and lemon soup, oxtail soup, fish soup, rice soup, lentil soup, minestrone, cherry sou

entries.label: prepared salad (eurofir)
entries.definition: A combination of one or more vegetable, fruit, herb, meat, poultry, seafood, egg, cereal or pasta, usually served with some kind of moist dressing; may be moulded with a jellying agent. Salad takes precedence over other product types. Examples are egg salad, tuna salad, mixed vegetable salad, jelled fruit salad, macaroni salad, potato salad, rice salad, mayonnaise salad.

entries.label: sandwich filling (eurofir)
entries.definition: Includes cheese-based sandwich filling, fish-based sandwich filling.

entries.label: savoury snack (eurofir)
entries.definition: Unsweetened food product marketed for consumption between meals; excludes nuts, edible seeds, and sweetened products such as cakes, puddings and candies. Examples are potato crisps, maize-based snacks, pretzels, popcorn.

entries.label: succotash

Other ingredients may be added including tomatoes, green or sweet red peppers, and okra. Combining a grain with a legume provides a dish that is high in all essential amino acids.

entries.label: garden snail

entries.label: sweet onion plant
entries.definition: Sweet onion is a variety of onion that is not pungent. There are several varieties of sweet onion. The term sweet onion comes from the perceived sweetness of the onion compared to other varieties. This perceived sweetness is derived from a low sulfur content and and high water content when compared to other onion varieties.

entries.label: yellow onion plant
entries.definition: The brown onion or yellow onion (*Allium cepa *L.) is a variety of dry onion with a strong flavour. Use the broad term *SUGAR* only if the specific sugar used is not known or not listed in the vocabulary.

entries.label: food supplement form
entries.definition: Food supplements are generally marketed in dose form designed to be taken in measured small unit quantities, such as pill, capsule, tablet, powder or liquid.

entries.label: edible tablet
entries.definition: A tablet is a mixture of active substances and excipients, usually in powder form, pressed or compacted into a solid. Tablets can be made in virtually any shape, although requirements of patients and tableting machines mean that most are round, oval or capsule shaped. entries.label: chewable tablet
entries.definition: Chewable tablets are the tablets which are required to be broken and chewed in between the teeth before ingestion. These tablets are given to the children who have difficulty in swallowing and to the adults who dislike swallowing. A number of antacid tablets and multivitamin tablets are prepared as chewable tablets. [http://www.pharmpedia.com/Chewable_tablets]

entries.label: effervescent tablet
entries.definition: Effervescent tablets are uncoated tablets that generally contain acid substances and carbonates or bicarbonates and which react rapidly in the presence of water by releasing carbon dioxide. They are intended to be dissolved or dispersed in water before use. [http://www.pharmpedia.com/Effervescent_tablet]

entries.label: edible capsule

entries.label: individual regular diet
entries.definition: A descriptive diet which is the regular course of eating and drinking adopted by an organism.

entries.label: study intervention diet
entries.definition: A diet administered during an intervention study. It usually comprises the adoption of a certain nutritional intervention, intended as the prescription of consuming or not consuming certain food, and follows a precise study design. Intervention studies usually compare at least two subgroups of a population, one control group receiving a null nutritional intervention, and one or more test groups re

entries.label: clinically prescribed diet
entries.definition: A diet prescribed by a physician/ nutritionist to meet specific nutritional needs of a person.

entries.label: population regular diet
entries.definition: A descriptive diet consumed by a population in a certain geographical area, or in a certain cultural setting, or following certain common eating behaviour.

entries.label: diet
entries.definition: A collection of food types or items which have organoleptic, nutritional, availability, safety, meal time, or socially relevant characteristics with respect to a consuming individual or population.

entries.label: diet by digestive capability
entries.definition: A diet that is defined by the biological, anatomical, and evolutionistic digestive capabilities of a given organism.

entries.label: diet by type of food
entries.definition: A diet that is defined by characteristics of ingested food.

entries.label: diet by agricultural treatment
entries.definition: A diet which involves food produced under certain agricultural conditions.

entries.label: diet by nutritional composition
entries.definition: A diet defined by the nutritional presence or absence of types of food bioactive compounds.

entries.label: restrictive diet
entries.definition: An eating pattern that excludes a given diet.

entries.label: prescribed diet
entries.definition: A diet which is prescribed to meet some dietary pattern objective for an individual organism or group.

entries.label: descriptive diet
entries.definition: A diet which represents food types or items consumed in the regular course of eating and drinking by an individual or population over some duration of time.

entries.label: recommended diet
entries.definition: A prescribed diet which pertains to a population or sub-population of organism.

entries.label: carnivorous diet
entries.definition: A diet of a carnivore, which focuses almost exclusively on the consumption of animal food sources.

entries.label: omnivorous diet
entries.definition: A diet of an omivore, which includes both plant and animal food sources.

entries.label: herbivorous diet
entries.definition: A diet of a herbivore, which focuses almost exclusively on the consumption of plants, fungi and/or lichen.

entries.label: diet by food organism
entries.definition: A diet defined by the food source organisms it allows or excludes.

entries.label: vegetarian diet
entries.definition: A diet which focuses almost exclusively on the consumption of plants, fungi and/or lichen.

entries.label: vegan diet
entries.definition: A diet that excludes all animal products (including fish and seafood).

entries.label: lacto-vegetarian diet
entries.definition: A diet that includes vegetarian and milk-derived food.

entries.label: ovo-vegetarian diet
entries.definition: A diet that includes vegetarian and avian egg derived food.

entries.label: lacto-ovo vegetarian diet
entries.definition: A diet that includes vegetarian, avian egg, and milk derived food.

entries.label: semi-vegetarian diet
entries.definition: primarily a plant-based diet but includes meat, dairy, eggs, poultry and fish on occasion or in small quantities

entries.label: pescetarian diet
entries.definition: A diet which includes vegetarian food as well as fish and seafood.

entries.label: non-beef diet
entries.definition: A diet that excludes food containing beef food products.

entries.label: non-pork diet
entries.definition: A diet that excludes food containing swine food products.

entries.label: infant breast milk diet
entries.definition: A diet consisting entirely of breast milk.

entries.label: infant formula milk diet
entries.definition: A diet involving formula milk.

entries.label: diet by food texture
entries.definition: A diet defined by the texture of prepared food.

entries.label: texture modified diet
entries.definition: A diet containing carefully selected foods of an appropriate consistency which can be more easily chewed and managed by a person with dysphagia.

entries.label: liquid diet
entries.definition: A full liquid diet is made up only of fluids and foods that are normally liquid and foods that turn to liquid when they are at room temperature. A full liquid diet excludes solid foods.

entries.label: organic agriculture diet
entries.definition: A diet consisting of food produced from organic agriculture (food that is grown without the use of synthetic fertilizers, sewage sludge, irradiation, genetic engineering, pesticides, or drugs.)

entries.label: non-organic agriculture diet
entries.definition: A diet consisting of food that may have been reared with the use of pesticides, herbicides or chemical fertilizers.

entries.label: ketogenic diet
entries.definition: A ketogenic diet is a high-fat, low-carbohydrate, adequate-protein diet that mimics a fasting state, resulting in the substitution of ketone bodies as a source of energy. The ketogenic diet can be used to reduce recurrent epileptic seizures in individuals with intractable epilepsy. Intractable epilepsy is defined as epilepsy that failed to respond to three or more antiepileptic drugs. A high-fat,

entries.label: DASH diet
entries.definition: Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) trial, which demonstrated that consuming a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy products and reduced in saturated fat and cholesterol

entries.label: mediterranean diet
entries.definition: A moderate-fat, restricted-calorie, Mediterranean diet is rich in vegetables and low in red meat, with poultry and fish replacing beef and lamb.

entries.label: high-carbohydrate diet
entries.definition: A diet which provides > 60% of total dietary energy from carbohydrates.  It consists predominantly of high glycemic carbohydrates have detrimental metabolic effects

entries.label: low-carbohydrate, high-protien, high fat diet

entries.definition: Low-carbohydrate diets restrict carbohydrate consumption relative to the average diet. entries.label: high fat diet
entries.definition: A diet involving the a larger proportion of fat than normal.

entries.label: low fat diet
entries.definition: A restricted-energy diet with less than 30% of energy from fat.

entries.label: gluten free diet
entries.definition: A diet which minimises or eliminates the consumption of gluten.

entries.label: self-prescribed diet
entries.definition: A diet that an individual organism has chosen as an objective.

entries.label: research prescribed diet
entries.definition: A diet prescribed to a group in a research study.

entries.label: study null nutritional diet
entries.definition: A dietairy pattern adhered to by a study control group. (possibly a placebo).

entries.label: coeliac diet
entries.definition: A diet designed to reduce the symptoms of Coeliac disease which is caused by a reaction to gliadin (a gluten protein found in wheat) and similar proteins found in other crops.

entries.label: FODMAP diet
entries.definition: A diet involving the avoidance of Fermentable Oligo-Di-Monosaccharides and Polyols.

entries.label: weight loss diet
entries.definition: A diet designed to reduce the presence of fat in an organism.

entries.label: performance diet
entries.definition: A diet which has an athletic performance objective

entries.label: ethnographic diet
entries.definition: A cultural or religious eating pattern.

entries.label: halal diet
entries.definition: A diet consisting of halal approved food.

entries.label: kosher diet
entries.definition: A diet consisting of kosher approved food.

entries.label: self-reported diet
entries.definition: An ingested food data set which is subjectively recorded or recalled by an individual consuming the food.

entries.label: objectively-reported diet
entries.definition: A descriptive diet which is observed by a researcher to have been consumed by a subject organism or population of organisms.

entries.label: ingested food data set
entries.definition: A descriptive diet which contains a list of foods that an individual organism has ingested over some period of time.

entries.label: NCI usual diet
entries.definition: A population regular diet which is a long-term average daily intake of nutrients and/or foods calculated according to a National Cancer Institute statistical model.

entries.label: ingested food log
entries.definition: An ingested food data set of food consumption events detailing food ingested and the time of ingestion.

entries.label: daily food intake
entries.definition: A descriptive diet containing food types or items pertinent to an average day or a given day which are ingested by an individual or organism population. The collection may indicate quantities or counts of food material.

entries.label: daily average nutritional intake
entries.definition: A descriptive diet containing nutrient classes and their average daily intake quantity for an individual or organism population.

entries.label: dietary regimen
entries.definition: A set of restrictions on food type ingestion and/or timing of food ingestion.

entries.label: globalized diet
entries.definition: the diet resulting from the lifestyle adaptation following the industrial revolution. It is often associated with western countries, but is increasingly becoming adopted also in other geographic areas. entries.label: rural diet
entries.definition: the diet characteristic of the lifestyle in isolated/rural areas, commonly in developing countries. It is mainly composed of naturally available food products, including fresh animal protein and vegetables while excluding industrially processed foods. entries.label: carotenoids
entries.definition: Carotenoids are yellow, orange, and red organic pigments that are produced by plants and algae, as well as several bacteria and fungi. Carotenoids from the diet are stored in the fatty tissues of animals. There is insufficient evidence to state that carotenoids have an antioxidant function in humans or that carotenoid dietary supplements lower the risk of or prevent diseases.

entries.label: paprika oleoresin
entries.definition: PAPRIKA OLEORESIN (also known as PAPRIKA EXTRACT and oleoresin paprika) is an oil-soluble extract from the fruits of Capsicum annuum or Capsicum frutescens, and is primarily used as a colouring and/or flavouring in food products.

entries.label: Glycerol monostearate
entries.definition: GLYCEROL MONOSTEARATE, commonly known as GMS, is a monoglyceride commonly used as an emulsifier in foods. GMS is a food additive used as a thickening, emulsifying, anticaking, and preservative agent; an emulsifying agent for oils, waxes, and solvents; a protective coating for hygroscopic powders; a solidifier and control release agent in pharmaceuticals; and a resin lubricant.

entries.label: gelatin
entries.definition: GELATIN or GELATINE is a translucent, colorless, brittle (when dry), flavorless food ingredient that is derived from collagen obtained from various animal body parts.

entries.label: citrus pectin
entries.definition: Modified citrus pectin (also known as CITRUS PECTIN, Pecta-Sol and MCP) is a modified, more digestible form of pectin. It is obtained from the peels, seeds and pulp of citrus fruits using a chemical extraction process.

entries.definition: FERMENT is an agent, such as an enzyme, bacterium, or fungus, that brings about fermentation.

entries.label: microbial culture
entries.definition: A microbiological culture, or microbial culture, is a method of multiplying microbial organisms by letting them reproduce in predetermined culture medium under controlled laboratory conditions. All cultures in food are microbial cultures

entries.label: lactic ferments
entries.definition: Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are an order of gram-positive, low-GC, acid-tolerant, generally nonsporulating, nonrespiring, either rod-shaped (bacilli) or spherical (cocci) bacteria that share common metabolic and physiological characteristics.

entries.label: bifidus
entries.definition: BIFIDOBACTERIUM is a genus of gram-positive, nonmotile, often branched anaerobic bacteria. They are ubiquitous inhabitants of the gastrointestinal tract, vagina and mouth of mammals humans.

entries.label: Bifidobacterium bifidum
entries.definition: BIFIDOBACTERIUM BIFIDUM is a bacterial species of the genus Bifidobacterium. B. bifidum is one of the most common probiotic bacteria that can be found in the body of mammals, including humans.

entries.label: Bifidobacterium lactis
entries.definition: BIFIDOBACTERIUM ANIMALIS is a gram-positive, anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium of the Bifidobacterium genus which can be found in the large intestines of humans. Both old names B. animalis and B. lactis are still used on product labels, as this species is frequently used as a probiotic. In most cases, which subspecies is used in the product is not clear. Several companies have attempted to trademark

entries.label: Bifidobacterium longum
entries.definition: BIFIDOBACTERIUM LONGUM is a Gram-positive, catalase-negative, rod-shaped bacterium present in the human gastrointestinal tract. B. longum is non-pathogenic and is often added to food products.

entries.label: bifidus actiregularis
entries.definition: Danone decided to add a probiotic strain: BIFIDUS ACTIREGULARIS. Activia products thus contain Bifidobacterium animalis DN 173,010, a proprietary strain of Bifidobacterium, a probiotic which is marketed by Dannon under the trade names Bifidus Regularis, Bifidus Actiregularis, Bifidus Digestivum and Bifidobacterium Lactis.

entries.label: Lactobacillus
entries.definition: LACTOBACILLUS is a genus of Gram-positive, facultative anaerobic or microaerophilic, rod-shaped, non-spore-forming bacteria. Lactobacillus is the most common probiotic found in food such as yogurt, and it is diverse in its application to maintain human well-being. Some Lactobacillus species are used as starter cultures in industry for controlled fermentation in the production of wine, yogurt, chee

entries.label: Lactobacillus acidophilus
entries.definition: LACTOBACILLUS ACIDOPHILUS is a species of gram positive bacteria in the genus Lactobacillus. L. acidophilus is a homofermentative, microaerophilic species, fermenting sugars into lactic acid. These strains are commercially used in many dairy products in the production of acidophilus-type yogurt.

entries.label: Lactobacillus bulgaricus
entries.definition: LACTOBACILLUS DELBRUECKII SUBSP. BULGARICUS (until 2014 known as Lactobacillus bulgaricus) is the main bacteria used for the production of yogurt.

entries.label: lactobacillus casei
entries.definition: LACTOBACILLUS CASEI is a species of genus Lactobacillus found in the human urinary tract and mouth. The most common application of L. casei is industrial, specifically for dairy production.

entries.label: Lactobacillus Helveticus
entries.definition: LACTOBACILLUS HELVETICUS is a lactic-acid producing, rod-shaped bacterium of the genus Lactobacillus. It is most commonly used in the production of American Swiss cheese and Emmental cheese, but is also sometimes used in making other styles of cheese, such as Cheddar, Parmesan, Romano, provolone, and mozzarella.

entries.label: Lactobacillus reuteri
entries.definition: LACTOBACILLUS REUTERI is a Gram-positive bacterium that naturally inhabits the gut of mammals and birds. Although L. reuteri occurs naturally in humans, it is not found in all individuals. Dietary supplementation can sustain high levels of it in those with deficiencies.

entries.label: Lactobacillus rhamnosus
entries.definition: LACTOBACILLUS RHAMNOSUS sometimes is used in yogurt and dairy products such as fermented and unpasteurized milk and semi-hard cheese.

entries.label: Lactiplantibacillus
entries.definition: LACTIPLANTIBACILLUS is a genus of lactic acid bacteria

entries.label: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum
entries.definition: LACTIPLANTIBACILLUS PLANTARUM is a widespread member of the genus Lactiplantibacillus, commonly found in many fermented food products

entries.label: Bacillus coagulans
entries.definition: BACILLUS COAGULANS is a lactic acid-forming bacterial species. B. coagulans is often marketed as Lactobacillus sporogenes or a 'sporeforming lactic acid bacterium' probiotic, but this is an outdated name due to taxonomic changes in 1939.

entries.label: Streptococcus thermophilus
entries.definition: STREPTOCOCCUS THERMOPHILUS also known as Streptococcus salivarius subsp. thermophilus is a gram-positive bacterium, and a fermentative facultative anaerobe, of the viridans group. It is also classified as a lactic acid bacterium.

entries.label: enzyme
entries.definition: ENZYME - is a macromolecular biological catalysts. Enzymes accelerate chemical reactions.

entries.label: rennet
entries.definition: RENNET is a complex set of enzymes produced in the stomachs of ruminant mammals. Chymosin, its key component, is a protease enzyme that curdles the casein in milk.

entries.label: animal-based rennet
entries.definition: CALF RENNET is extracted from the inner mucosa of the fourth stomach chamber (the abomasum) of young, unweaned calves as part of livestock butchering.

entries.label: calf rennet
entries.definition: CALF RENNET is extracted from the inner mucosa of the fourth stomach chamber (the abomasum) of young, unweaned calves as part of livestock butchering.

entries.label: microbial rennet
entries.definition: Some molds such as Rhizomucor miehei are able to produce proteolytic enzymes. Cheeses produced this way are suitable for vegetarians, provided no animal-based alimentation was used during the production.

entries.label: cellulase
entries.definition: CELLULASE is any of several enzymes produced chiefly by fungi, bacteria, and protozoans that catalyze cellulolysis, the decomposition of cellulose and of some related polysaccharides. Cellulase is used for commercial food processing in coffee.

entries.label: Lactase

entries.label: caribou
entries.definition: "Caribou" is the term used in North America (Canada, Alaska) for wild populations. "Reindeer" is used in Europe and Asia, and also refers to the domesticated populations found especially in places like Scandinavia and Russia.

entries.label: chuck steak
entries.definition: CHUCK STEAK is a cut of beef and is part of the sub-prime cut known as the chuck.

entries.label: lamb
entries.definition: LAMB, hogget and mutton are the meat of domestic sheep (species Ovis aries) at different ages. The meat of a lamb is taken from the animal between one month and one year old, with a carcase (carcass in American English) weight of between 5.5 and 30 kg. This meat generally is more tender than that from older sheep and appears more often on tables in some Western countries.

entries.label: rabbit
entries.definition: RABBITS are small mammals in the family Leporidae of the order Lagomorpha. In some areas, wild rabbits and hares are hunted for their meat, a lean source of high quality protein. Domesticated descendants of the European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) that are bred and kept as livestock account for the estimated 200 million tons of rabbit meat produced annually.

entries.label: sheep
entries.definition: Domestic sheep (Ovis aries) are quadrupedal, ruminant mammals typically kept as livestock.  Sheep are raised for fleeces, meat (lamb, hogget or mutton) , fat and milk.

entries.label: mutton
entries.definition: mutton is the meat of domestic sheep (species Ovis aries). The meat of an adult sheep is mutton, a term only used for the meat, not the living animals. Meat from sheep features prominently in several cuisines of the Mediterranean.

entries.label: reindeer
entries.definition: "Reindeer" is used in Europe and Asia, and also refers to the domesticated populations found especially in places like Scandinavia and Russia. "Caribou" is the term used in North America (Canada, Alaska) for wild populations.

entries.label: meat patty
entries.definition: A MEAT PATTY is a flattened, usually round, serving of ground meat.

entries.label: goat meat
entries.definition: GOAT MEAT or goat's meat is the meat of the domestic goat (Capra aegagrus hircus). Goat meat is savory and less sweet than beef[9] but slightly sweeter than lamb. It can be prepared in a variety of ways, such as being stewed, curried, baked, grilled, barbecued, minced, canned, fried, or made into sausage. Goat jerky is also another popular variety.

entries.label: pork shoulder
entries.definition: Als Schweinebug (auch Schweineschulter) wird das Vorderbein vom Schwein bezeichnet. Es befindet sich direkt neben dem Schweinenacken.

entries.label: pork rind
entries.definition: Pork rind is the culinary term for the skin of a pig.

entries.label: bacon
entries.definition: Bacon is a type of salt-cured pork. Bacon is prepared from several different cuts of meat, typically from the pork belly or from back cuts, which have less fat than the belly. It is eaten on its own, as a side dish (particularly in breakfasts), or used as a minor ingredient to flavour dishes

entries.label: barde
entries.definition: La BARDE est une fine tranche de lard gras frais, de lard salé ou de lard fumé avec laquelle on enveloppe divers morceaux de viandes, fruits ou légumes pour garder leur texture moelleuse et éviter le dessèchement.

entries.label: lardon
entries.definition: A LARDON, also called lardoon or larding, is a small strip or cube of fatty bacon, or pork fat (usually subcutaneous fat) used in a wide variety of cuisines to flavor savory foods and salads.

entries.label: boston butt
entries.definition: BOSTON BUTT, or pork butt, is the American name for a cut of pork that comes from the upper part of the shoulder from the front leg and may contain the blade bone.  Boston butt is the most common cut used for pulled pork, a staple of barbecue in the southern United States.

entries.label: lard
entries.definition: LARD is fat from a pig, in both its rendered and unrendered forms. Lard is one of the few edible oils with a relatively high smoke point, attributable to its high saturated fatty acids content. Pure lard is especially useful for cooking since it produces little smoke when heated and has a distinct flavor when combined with other foods.

entries.label: collagen
entries.definition: COLLAGEN is the main structural protein in the extracellular space in the various connective tissues in the body.  It is widely used in the form of collagen casings for sausages, which are also used in the manufacture of musical strings.

entries.label: rice starch
entries.definition: Rice starch is derived from rice grains (Oryza sativa), one of the world's most widely cultivated cereal crops, grown extensively across Asia, and increasingly in parts of the Americas and Europe. entries.label: oil and fat
entries.definition: Several edible vegetable and animal oils, and also fats, are used for various purposes in cooking and food preparation. In particular, many foods are fried in oil much hotter than boiling water. Oils are also used for flavoring and for modifying the texture of foods (e.g. Stir Fry). Cooking oils are derived either from animal fat, as butter, lard and other types, or plant oils from the olive, maiz

entries.label: vegetable oil and fat
entries.definition: VEGETABLE OILS, or vegetable fats, are fats extracted from seeds, or less often, from other parts of fruits.

entries.label: oil
entries.definition: Cooking OIL is plant, animal, or synthetic fat used in frying, baking, and other types of cooking. It is also used in food preparation and flavouring not involving heat, such as salad dressings and bread dips, and in this sense might be more accurately termed edible oil.

entries.label: hydrogenated oil
entries.definition: Hydrogenation converts liquid vegetable oils into solid or semi-solid fats, such as those present in margarine. Changing the degree of saturation of the fat changes some important physical properties, such as the melting range, which is why liquid oils become semi-solid.

entries.label: fat
entries.definition: FAT is one of the three main macronutrients, along with the other two:carbohydrate and protein. Fats molecules consist of primarily carbon and hydrogen atoms, thus they are all hydrocarbon molecules.

entries.label: animal fat
entries.definition: ANIMAL FATS and oils are lipid materials derived from animals. Physically, oils are liquid at room temperature, and fats are solid. Although many animal parts and secretions may yield oil, in commercial practice, oil is extracted primarily from rendered tissue fats obtained from livestock animals like pigs, chickens and cows.

entries.label: butterfat
entries.definition: BUTTERFAT - the fatty portion of milk.

entries.label: clarified butter
entries.definition: CLARIFIED BUTTER is milk fat rendered from butter to separate the milk solids and water from the butterfat

entries.label: ghee
entries.definition: Ghee is a type of clarified butter that's especially common in South Asian and Indian cooking. It has a rich, nutty, slightly caramelized taste. It's used in Indian cooking (dals, curries, rice dishes), for frying, drizzling over flatbreads.

entries.label: camelina oil

entries.label: cocoa butter

entries.label: canola oil
entries.definition: Canola oil, or canola for short, originally known as low erucic acid rapeseed, is a vegetable oil derived from a variety of rapeseed bred in Canada (Saskatchewan and Manitoba, 1960s-1970s) to be low in erucic acid, as opposed to colza oil.

entries.label: apple cider vinegar
entries.definition: CIDER VINEGAR, a vinegar made from apples, sugar and yeast

entries.label: balsamic vinegar
entries.definition: Balsamic vinegar is a very dark, concentrated, and intensely flavoured vinegar originating in Italy, made wholly or partially from grape must, grape juice with all the skins, seeds and stems.

entries.label: rice vinegar
entries.definition: RICE VINEGAR is a vinegar made from fermented rice

entries.label: ethanol
entries.definition: ETHANOL, also called alcohol, ethyl alcohol, grain alcohol, and drinking alcohol, is a chemical compound, a simple alcohol with the chemical formula C2H5OH.

entries.label: liqueur
entries.definition: A liqueur is an alcoholic drink flavored variously by fruits, herbs, spices, flowers, nuts or cream combined with distilled spirits.

entries.label: amaretto
entries.definition: Amaretto (Italian for "a little bitter") is a sweet Italian liqueur that originated in Saronno, Italy.

entries.label: gin
entries.definition: GIN is a distilled alcoholic drink that derives its predominant flavour from juniper berries.

entries.label: champagne
entries.definition: Champagne is sparkling wine or, in the EU countries, legally only that sparkling wine which comes from the Champagne region of France.

entries.label: pomace brandy
entries.definition: Pomace brandy is a liquor distilled from pomace that is left over from winemaking, after the grapes are pressed.

entries.label: kirsch
entries.definition: A kirschwasser or kirsch is a clear, colorless fruit brandy traditionally made from double distillation of morello cherries, a dark-colored cultivar of the sour cherry.

entries.label: tequila
entries.definition: TEQUILA is a regional distilled beverage and type of alcoholic drink made from the blue agave plant, primarily in the area surrounding the city of Tequila

entries.label: wine
entries.definition: WINE is an alcoholic beverage made from fermented grapes.

entries.label: sparkling wine
entries.definition: SPARKLING WINE is a wine with significant levels of carbon dioxide in it, making it fizzy. Sparkling wine is usually either white or rosé, but there are examples of red sparkling wines.

entries.label: white wine
entries.definition: WHITE WINE is a wine whose colour can be straw-yellow, yellow-green, or yellow-gold.

entries.label: muscadet
entries.definition: MUSCADET is a French white wine.

entries.label: red wine
entries.definition: RED WINE is a type of wine made from dark-colored (black) grape varieties. The actual color of the wine can range from intense violet, typical of young wines, through to brick red for mature wines and brown for older red wines. The juice from most purple grapes is greenish-white, the red color coming from anthocyan pigments present in the skin of the grape

entries.label: sauternes
entries.definition: Sauternes is a French sweet wine from the Sauternais region of the Graves section in Bordeaux.

entries.label: rosé wine
entries.definition: A ROSÉ is a type of wine that incorporates some of the color from the grape skins, but not enough to qualify it as a red wine.

entries.label: liqueur wine
entries.definition: Fortified wine is a wine to which a distilled spirit, usually brandy, is added. Many different styles of fortified wine have been developed, including Port, Sherry, Madeira, Marsala, Commandaria wine, and the aromatised wine Vermouth.

entries.label: Madeira
entries.definition: MADEIRA is a fortified wine made on the Portuguese Madeira Islands, off the coast of Africa. Madeira is produced in a variety of styles ranging from dry wines which can be consumed on their own as an aperitif to sweet wines usually consumed with dessert.

entries.label: Marsala wine
entries.definition: MARSALA is a wine, dry or sweet, produced in the region surrounding the Italian city of Marsala in Sicily.

entries.label: port
entries.definition: PORT wine (also known as vinho do Porto, Porto, and usually simply port) is a Portuguese fortified wine produced with distilled grape spirits exclusively in the Douro Valley in the northern provinces of Portugal.

entries.label: sherry
entries.definition: SHERRY is a fortified wine made from white grapes that are grown near the city of Jerez de la Frontera in Andalusia, Spain. Sherry is produced in a variety of styles made primarily from the Palomino grape, ranging from light versions similar to white table wines, such as Manzanilla and fino, to darker and heavier versions that have been allowed to oxidise as they age in barrel, such as Amontillado

entries.label: brandy
entries.definition: BRANDY is a spirit produced by distilling wine. Brandy generally contains 35–60% alcohol by volume (70–120 US proof) and is typically consumed as an after-dinner digestif.

entries.label: vermouth
entries.definition: A dry, or sweet apéritif wine flavored with aromatic herbs, and often used in mixed drinks.

entries.label: absinthe
entries.definition: ABSINTHE is historically described as a distilled, highly alcoholic beverage

entries.label: sorghum

entries.label: triticale
entries.definition: Triticale is a hybrid grain bred by crossing wheat and rye, first developed in the late 19th century and refined for commercial use in Europe through the 20th century. entries.label: wheat
entries.definition: WHEAT is a grass widely cultivated for its seed.

entries.label: whole wheat kernels
entries.definition: Whole wheat grain (Triticum aestivum) is the raw, unprocessed wheat kernel — bran, germ, and endosperm all intact, unmilled. Cultivated for over 8,000 years since its Fertile Crescent origins, it's the source grain from which both atta and maida are later produced. Raw, it has a hard, chewy texture with an earthy, nutty taste; when cracked (dalia) or sprouted, it becomes softer and slightly sweet.

entries.label: soft white wheat
entries.definition: Soft white wheat is a low-protein variety grown mainly in the Pacific Northwest, California, and parts of the Midwest, prized for its adaptability to temperate climates. entries.label: soft red winter wheat

entries.label: durum wheat

entries.label: hard red spring wheat
entries.definition: Hard red spring wheat is grown mainly in the northern U.S. Great Plains and Canada, planted in spring and harvested in fall due to the region's harsh winters. entries.label: hard red winter wheat

It has a robust, slightly nutty, earthy flavor with more depth than white wheat varieties. Its high protein and gluten content make it a top choice for yeasted breads, as well as all-purpose and bread flours.

entries.label: hard white wheat

Nutritionally, it's high in fiber and B vitamins, with a lower glycemic impact than wheat.

entries.label: date
entries.definition: DATE, the fruit of the date palm (Phoenix dactylifera). Dry or soft dates are eaten out-of-hand, or may be pitted and stuffed with fillings such as almonds, walnuts, pecans, candied orange and lemon peel, tahini, marzipan or cream cheese.

entries.label: feijoa
entries.definition: Feijoa (Acca sellowiana) is a fruit native to South America — specifically the highlands of southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, and northern Argentina. The flavour is distinctive and hard to compare — often described as a mix of pineapple, guava, mint, and strawberry, with floral notes. The flesh inside is creamy white and slightly gritty near the center, similar to a ripe pear.

entries.label: horned melon
entries.definition: The horned melon (kiwano) is a tropical fruit native to sub-Saharan Africa, though it's now grown in other warm regions like New Zealand, Australia, and California. The flavor is mild and refreshing — often described as a blend of cucumber, banana, and lime, with a slightly tart note.

entries.label: java plum
entries.definition: Java plum (Syzygium cumini) is a tropical evergreen tree in the myrtle family (Myrtaceae), making it more closely related to cloves and eucalyptus than to actual plums.

entries.label: jujube
entries.definition: Jujube (also called Chinese date or red date) is a small fruit from the Ziziphus jujuba tree, native to China but now grown throughout Asia, the Middle East, and parts of Europe and America. Fresh jujubes taste crisp and mildly sweet, similar to an apple.

entries.label: kiwifruit
entries.definition: KIWIFRUIT (often abbreviated as KIWI), or Chinese gooseberry is the edible berry of several species of woody vines in the genus Actinidia.

entries.label: lychee
entries.definition: LYCHEE is the sole member of the genus Litchi in the soapberry family, Sapindaceae.

entries.label: cantaloupe
entries.definition: Cantaloupe (muskmelon, mushmelon, rockmelon, sweet melon) or spanspek (South Africa) is a variety of the Cucumis melo species in the Cucurbitaceae family.

entries.label: nance
entries.definition: Nance is a small tropical fruit native to Central America, the Caribbean, and parts of South America. Small, round, yellow to orange berries, about 1–2 cm in diameter, growing in clusters. It has a very distinctive, pungent aroma and a flavor that's a unique mix of sweet, sour, and slightly cheesy or fermented.

entries.label: naranjilla
entries.definition: Naranjilla is a tropical fruit native to South America, mainly grown in Ecuador, Colombia, and Peru. Small to medium round fruit, about the size of a golf ball with bright orange skin covered in fine, removable fuzz. The flavor is very distinctive — a unique mix of tart, citrusy, and tropical, often described as a cross between pineapple, lime, and rhubarb.

entries.label: white brugnon
entries.definition: Native to China, brugnons spread along ancient trade routes into Persia and the Mediterranean, where Mediterranean climates now support major cultivation. The white-fleshed variety offers a delicate, low-acid sweetness compared to yellow varieties, with smooth, fuzz-free skin and flesh that clings to the pit. Consumed fresh as a snack or dessert fruit, it also features in salads, tarts, and preser

entries.label: Garofa nectarine
entries.definition: Yellow-fleshed early season nectarine variety.

entries.label: ōhelo berry
entries.definition: ʻŌhelo is a small, native Hawaiian shrub in the cranberry family, commonly found at high elevations on the islands of Maui and Hawaiʻi. Ōhelo is related to the cranberry but much less tart — mildly sweet and mildly tart, with a texture similar to cranberries or blueberries.

entries.label: pitanga
entries.definition: Pitanga is a tropical fruit native to South America. The fruit is a berry with a persistent calyx up to 4 cm in diameter and eight clearly visible ribs. Its color changes from green to orange and purple as it matures. The flavor is unique — peppery and fruity, and quite complex

entries.label: bullocks heart
entries.definition: Native to the Caribbean and Central America, but now grown across tropical regions of South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Africa. The flesh inside is white to pale yellow, soft, and creamy, though generally considered less refined in flavor than its relatives

entries.label: prickly pear
entries.definition: Fruit from plants in the Opuntia (or prickly pear cactus) genus.

entries.label: rose apple
entries.definition: A rose apple (Syzygium jambos or related species) is a tropical fruit native to Southeast Asia and the Indian subcontinent. Despite its name, it's not related to either roses or apples — it belongs to the myrtle family. Pear- or bell-shaped fruit, usually pale yellow, white, pink, or red, with a waxy, smooth skin. Mildly sweet with a subtle floral aroma reminiscent of roses.

entries.label: rowal
entries.definition: Rowal (scientific name Pangium edule) is a tropical fruit native to Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands. The fruits are generally 15–30 cm long, with a rough brown exterior. The flesh has a strong aroma. The fresh fruit and seeds contain hydrogen cyanide and are DEADLY POISONOUS if consumed without prior preparation.

entries.label: sapodilla
entries.definition: Sapodilla (Manilkara zapota) is a tropical fruit native to southern Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean. It's a small to medium-sized fruit with rough, brown, potato-like skin. The flesh inside is yellowish-brown, soft, and grainy in texture. Often described as one of the sweetest fruits in the world. It has a rich, caramel-like or brown sugar flavor, sometimes with hints of vanilla and pea

entries.label: soursop
entries.definition: Soursop is a tropical fruit from the Annona muricata tree, native to the Caribbean, Central America, and parts of South America and Africa. Large, green, spiky/prickly on the outside — it can weigh anywhere from 1 to 7 kg. The inside is white, creamy, and fibrous with large black seeds. It's taste is an unique blend of sweet and tangy — often described as a mix of strawberry, pineapple, and citrus

entries.label: sea-buckthorn
entries.definition: Hippophae rhamnoides, also known as SEA-BUCKTHORN is a species of flowering plant in the family Elaeagnaceae, native to the cold-temperate regions of Europe and Asia.

entries.label: sugar apple
entries.definition: A sugar apple (also called sweetsop) is a tropical fruit from the Annona squamosa tree, native to the tropical Americas and West Indies. It has a bumpy, knobby green skin made up of overlapping segments that look almost like scales or a pinecone. When ripe, the segments separate easily. The white, creamy flesh inside is sweet and custard-like — hence "sugar" apple. The taste is often described as

entries.label: grape
entries.definition: A grape is a fruit, botanically a berry, of the deciduous woody vines of the flowering plant genus Vitis.

entries.label: raisin
entries.definition: A RAISIN is a dried grape.

entries.label: sultana
entries.definition: SULTANA is a "white" (pale green), oval seedless grape variety also called the sultanina, Thompson Seedless, Lady de Coverly, and oval-fruited Kishmish.

entries.label: Corinthian raisins
entries.definition: Zante currants are small, dried, seedless grapes — despite the name, they're not actually related to fresh currants (which are berries from the Ribes genus). Dried fruits made from the Black Corinth grape.

entries.label: grape juice
entries.definition: Grape juice is obtained from crushing and blending grapes into a liquid.

entries.label: grape juice from concentrate
entries.definition: This is a compound product made of concentrate grape juice and water.

entries.label: must
entries.definition: Must is freshly crushed fruit juice (usually grape juice) that contains the skins, seeds, and stems of the fruit.

entries.label: chasselas
entries.definition: Chasselas or Chasselas blanc is a wine grape variety grown in Switzerland, France, Germany, Portugal, Hungary, Romania, New Zealand and Chile.

entries.label: poulsard
entries.definition: Poulsard (also Ploussard) is a red French wine grape variety from the Jura wine region.

entries.label: pošip
entries.definition: Pošip is an autochthonous white wine grape that is primarily grown in the Dalmatian region of Croatia on the island of Korčula, although small amounts are also being grown on the Pelješac Peninsula.

entries.label: sémillon
entries.definition: Sémillon is a golden-skinned grape used to make dry and sweet white wines, mostly in France and Australia.

entries.label: sylvaner
entries.definition: Sylvaner or Silvaner is a variety of white wine grape grown primarily in Alsace and Germany, where its official name is Grüner Silvaner.

entries.label: syrah
entries.definition: Syrah, also known as Shiraz, is a dark-skinned grape variety grown throughout the world and used primarily to produce red wine.

entries.label: teran
entries.definition: Teran grape is a variety of red grape from Istria, Croatia.

entries.label: bastardo
entries.definition: Trousseau or Trousseau Noir, also known as Bastardo, is an old variety of red wine grape originating in eastern France.

entries.label: strawberry guavas
entries.definition: Strawberry guava (Psidium cattleianum) is a tropical fruit tree native to eastern Brazil. The flesh is white to creamy, with a sweet-tart taste reminiscent of a mix between strawberry and guava — hence the name. It contains small, hard seeds.

entries.label: julienne mix
entries.definition: A mix of julienne cut vegetables.

entries.label: agathi leaves
entries.definition: Agathi leaves (Sesbania grandiflora) originate from South and Southeast Asia, where the tree grows widely across tropical and subtropical regions. The leaves have a mildly bitter, slightly grassy taste that softens when cooked. Culinarily, they're used in soups, stir-fries, lentil dishes, and traditional preparations across Indian, Sri Lankan, Thai, and Filipino cuisines, often paired with tamarin

entries.label: basella leaves
entries.definition: Basella alba, commonly called Malabar spinach or vine spinach, is a fast-growing climbing vine native to tropical Asia and Africa, now cultivated widely across South and Southeast Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean. Its thick, glossy leaves have a mild, slightly peppery taste and a mucilaginous texture similar to okra when cooked. Popular in stir-fries, soups, curries, and stews, it holds up well in

entries.label: bathua leaves
entries.definition: Bathua, also known as fat hen or lamb's quarters, is a wild leafy green native to Europe and Asia, now naturalized worldwide and especially prized in North Indian cuisine during winter months. Its leaves have an earthy, slightly tangy, spinach-like flavor with a tender texture when cooked. Traditionally used in soups, flatbreads (bathua paratha), raita, and sautéed side dishes, it's often paired w

entries.label: beet greens
entries.definition: Beet greens are the leafy tops of the beetroot plant (Beta vulgaris), native to the Mediterranean and Near East, where wild sea beet has been used since antiquity. They have an earthy, slightly bitter flavor with mild sweetness, similar to Swiss chard, and tender-crisp stems ranging from white to deep red. Widely used across Mediterranean, European, Middle Eastern, and South Asian cuisines, they a

entries.label: betel leaves
entries.definition: Betel leaf (Piper betle) is a heart-shaped, glossy leaf native to Southeast Asia, now cultivated across South and Southeast Asia and parts of the Pacific. It has a pungent, peppery, slightly bitter flavor with an aromatic, faintly numbing quality from natural essential oils. Globally, it's best known as the wrapper for paan, but is also used to wrap savory bites (as in Thai miang kham), chopped in

entries.label: chicory greens
entries.definition: Chicory greens are the leafy tops (and sometimes tender inner leaves) of the chicory plant (Cichorium intybus), a bitter leafy vegetable in the same family as endive and radicchio. They're used in cooking much like other bitter greens — think dandelion greens or escarole. Distinctly bitter, with a slight earthiness. The bitterness mellows a lot when cooked.

entries.label: collard greens
entries.definition: Collards (collard greens) are a leafy green vegetable in the cabbage family — the same species as kale, cabbage, and broccoli (Brassica oleracea), just bred for large, loose, dark green leaves rather than a tight head. Earthy, slightly bitter, and hearty — milder than mustard greens, tougher and more assertive than spinach. Traditionally slow-cooked (often with smoked meat, onion, garlic, vinegar,

entries.label: leafy tips cowpeas
entries.definition: Cowpea leafy tips (sometimes called cowpea leaves, or by local names like "kunde" in Swahili, "ewedu" relatives, or "bean leaves") are the young, tender shoot tips and leaves of the cowpea plant (Vigna unguiculata) — the same plant that produces black-eyed peas. While most people know cowpeas for their beans, the leaves are widely eaten as a leafy green vegetable in parts of Africa (especially Wes

entries.label: garland chrysanthemum
entries.definition: "Garland chrysanthemum" (also called tong ho in Chinese, shungiku in Japanese, and ssukgat in Korean) is an edible leafy green — not the ornamental flower you'd put in a bouquet, but a related plant (Glebionis coronaria) grown specifically for eating. Slightly bitter, herbal, and a little peppery — some describe it as tasting faintly like chrysanthemum tea smells.

entries.label: endive
entries.definition: Cichorium endivia is a species of flowering plant belonging to the genus Cichorium, which is widely cultivated as one of the species of similar bitter-leafed vegetables known as endive and escarole.

entries.label: dock
entries.definition: Dock (genus Rumex, especially curly dock — Rumex crispus — and broad-leaved dock — Rumex obtusifolius) is a wild edible plant. Young leaves have a tart, lemony, slightly sour flavor thanks to oxalic acid — similar to sorrel but a bit milder. As leaves mature they get tougher and more bitter/astringent. Young leaves: eaten raw in salads, or added to soups, stews, and sautés like spinach.; Older lea

entries.label: drumstick leaves
entries.definition: Small, oval-shaped leaflets of the moringa tree (Moringa oleifera), sometimes called the horseradish tree or ben tree. The leaves grow in clusters on the branches, often described as feathery or fern-like in arrangement. They're a popular vegetable in South Asian, Southeast Asian, and African cuisines. Added to salads, or cooked briefly like spinach — sautéed, added to soups, dals, or stir-fries.

entries.label: grape leaf
entries.definition: Grape leaves (also called vine leaves) are the young, tender leaves of the grape plant (Vitis vinifera), used as a vegetable or wrap in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Balkan, and Caucasian cooking rather than eaten as a leafy green on their own. Slightly tart, earthy, a bit lemony — this comes mostly from the way they're brined or cooked (often with lemon juice).

entries.label: fiddlehead fern
entries.definition: Fiddlehead ferns are the tightly coiled, immature fronds of certain fern species, harvested in early spring before they unfurl. They're named for their resemblance to the curled end (scroll) of a fiddle or violin. Most common edible variety: Ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris) is the safest and most widely eaten species. Not all fern fiddleheads are edible — some are toxic, so identification

entries.label: firewood leaf
entries.definition: Fireweed (Chamaenerion angustifolium, also called Epilobium angustifolium) is a tall wildflower with bright pink-purple flower spikes, common in northern temperate regions. Young leaves, picked before the plant flowers, can be eaten raw in salads or cooked like spinach. As the plant matures, the leaves get tougher and more bitter, so timing matters. Fireweed has a mild laxative effect in some peop

entries.label: radicchio
entries.definition: RADICCHIO is a perennial cultivated form of leaf chicory (Cichorium intybus, Asteraceae) sometimes known as Italian chicory because of its common use in Italian cuisine.

entries.label: broad-leaved endive
entries.definition: Escarole, or broad-leaved endive (var latifolia), has broad, pale green leaves and is less bitter than the other varieties. Varieties or names include Batavian endive, grumolo, scarola, and scarole.

entries.label: frillice iceberg lettuce
entries.definition: Frillice iceberg lettuce is a cross of curly endive and iceberg lettuce, with the taste and texture of iceberg and the frilly top of the curly endive.

entries.label: chard
entries.definition: CHARD (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris, Cicla-Group and Flavescens-Group) is a green leafy vegetable. Chard, like other green leafy vegetables, has highly nutritious leaves, making it a popular component of healthy diets.Fresh young chard can be used raw in salads. Mature chard leaves and stalks are typically cooked (like in pizzoccheri) or sautéed; the bitterness fades with cooking, leaving a refin

entries.label: potherb
entries.definition: The young, tender leaves of genus Corchorus (mainly Corchorus olitorius and Corchorus capsularis) are cooked and eaten as a green vegetable, similar to spinach or amaranth greens. When cooked, the leaves release a mucilaginous (slightly slimy) texture, somewhat like okra — this is prized in many cuisines for thickening soups and stews.

entries.label: mustard greens
entries.definition: Mustard greens are the leafy tops of the mustard plant (Brassica juncea), and they're a true member of the mustard family — grown specifically for their peppery, pungent leaves rather than for seeds or oil (though the same plant family produces mustard seeds too). Mustard greens have a distinctly sharp, spicy, peppery bite — similar to the kick you get from horseradish, wasabi, or arugula, but mor

entries.label: mustard spinach
entries.definition: Mustard spinach, also known as komatsuna, is a leafy green vegetable that's actually part of the mustard/brassica family (Brassica rapa var. perviridis) rather than being related to true spinach. It's an East Asian vegetable, especially popular in Japanese cuisine (where it's called komatsuna), though it's also grown and eaten in China and other parts of Asia. The flavor is mild and slightly peppe

entries.label: new zealand spinach
entries.definition: New Zealand spinach (Tetragonia tetragonioides) isn't a true spinach at all. it's eaten much the same way as regular spinach — the young leaves and shoot tips are harvested and used cooked (steamed, sautéed, boiled, or added to soups and stir-fries). It's usually not eaten raw in large quantities because of its oxalate content, and cooking also helps soften its slightly thicker, fuzzier texture.

entries.label: vine spinach
entries.definition: Vine spinach (also called Malabar spinach) is a tropical leafy green plant, not a true spinach but used similarly in cooking. It's especially popular in Indian, Filipino, and West African cooking, where it goes by various local names like poi saag (India) or slippery vegetable.

entries.label: water spinach
entries.definition: Water convolvulus (Ipomoea aquatica), also known as water spinach, morning glory, or kangkong, is a semi-aquatic tropical plant widely used as a leafy vegetable across Asia and Africa. It's a staple vegetable in cuisines across Southeast Asia (Vietnam, Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia). Both the leaves and tender stem tips are eaten, typically stir-fried with garlic, shrimp paste, or

entries.label: taro leaves
entries.definition: Across the Pacific and Caribbean, taro leaves show up in dishes like callaloo, and in parts of Asia and Africa they're simmered in coconut-based curries or soups. Raw taro leaves are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals, so they need thorough cooking.

entries.label: parsley
entries.definition: PARSLEY or garden parsley (Petroselinum crispum) is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae

entries.label: broccoli
entries.definition: BROCCOLI is an edible green plant in the cabbage family whose large flowering head is eaten as a vegetable.

entries.label: cauliflower
entries.definition: CAULIFLOWER is one of several vegetables in the species Brassica oleracea in the genus Brassica

entries.label: pointed cabbage
entries.definition: POINTED CABBAGE, also known as cone, sweetheart, hispi or sugarloaf cabbage is a form of cabbage (Brassica oleracea) with a tapering shape and large delicate leaves varying in colour from yellowish to blue-green. It tastes less pronounced and more delicate than common white cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata f. alba).

entries.label: red cabbage
entries.definition: Native to coastal Europe and cultivated worldwide since antiquity, red cabbage is a dense, round vegetable with deep purple-red leaves, colored by anthocyanin pigments that shift hue with soil acidity. Its flavor is peppery and slightly sweet when raw, mellowing into a tangy, earthy sweetness when cooked, often enhanced with vinegar or apples in European cuisines. Globally, it's eaten raw in salad

entries.label: Chinese cabbage
entries.definition: Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa subsp. pekinensis) originated in East Asia, likely China, and has been cultivated for over 1,500 years before spreading worldwide. It features pale green, crinkled leaves with wide white ribs and a mild, slightly sweet flavor with subtle peppery notes. Globally, it's used in stir-fries, soups, dumplings, salads, and most famously as the base for Korean kimchi; it als

entries.label: pak choi
entries.definition: Bok choy, pak choi or pok choi (Chinese:上海青; pinyin:Shànghǎi qīng; literally:"Shanghai Green"; Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis) is a type of Chinese cabbage.

entries.label: brussels sprouts
entries.definition: Brussels sprouts are small, leafy green vegetables belonging to the cabbage family, believed to have originated in Belgium, from which they take their name, though similar plants trace back to ancient Rome. They grow in tight, bud-like clusters along a thick stalk. Raw, they have a slightly bitter, peppery bite; cooked, they turn nuttier and sweeter, especially when roasted, caramelized, or charre

entries.label: kale
entries.definition: Kale originates from the eastern Mediterranean and Asia Minor, where it was cultivated by the ancient Greeks and Romans. Today it is grown worldwide, notably in Europe, North America, and parts of Asia and Africa. A hardy, cool-season crop, kale is sown by seed, thrives in temperate climates, tolerates frost, and is harvested by hand or machine as leaves mature. Its flavor is earthy, slightly bitt

entries.label: savoy cabbage
entries.definition: Green cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata) originated in the Mediterranean and Western Europe, cultivated from wild mustard plants over 2,000 years ago before spreading worldwide through trade and colonization. Today it's a staple across Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Americas. Its tightly packed, pale-green leaves offer a crisp texture and mild, slightly peppery flavor that turns sweeter when

entries.label: gai lan
entries.definition: Chinese broccoli (also called gai lan or kai lan, 芥蓝) is actually a distinct vegetable from regular broccoli, though they're related. Both belong to the Brassica oleracea species and the broader cabbage family. Gai lan has long, thick green stalks with flat, broad leaves and small, scattered flower buds. Western broccoli has a large, compact floret head on a thick stalk. It's slightly more bitter

entries.label: celery
entries.definition: CELERY (Apium graveolens) is a marshland plant in the family Apiaceae that has been cultivated as a vegetable since antiquity.

entries.label: fennel
entries.definition: FENNEL (Foeniculum vulgare) is a flowering plant species in the carrot family. The bulb, foliage, and fruits of the fennel plant are used in many of the culinary traditions of the world. The bulb is a crisp vegetable that can be sautéed, stewed, braised, grilled, or eaten raw. Young tender leaves are used for garnishes, as a salad, to add flavor to salads, to flavor sauces to be served with puddin

entries.label: rhubarb
entries.definition: RHUBARB is a cultivated plant in the genus Rheum in the family Polygonaceae. Rhubarb is stewed with sugar or used in pies and desserts, but it can also be put into savoury dishes or pickled. Rhubarb can be dehydrated and infused with fruit juice.

entries.label: arrowhead
entries.definition: Arrowhead (also called Sagittaria, water arrowhead, or 慈姑 cí gū in Chinese) is an aquatic plant whose starchy corms (bulb-like root tubers) are eaten as a vegetable. It grows in shallow ponds, marshes, and rice paddies, and is especially popular in Chinese, Japanese, and Southeast Asian cooking. Mildly bitter and slightly sweet, with a starchy texture similar to a chestnut or potato. The bitternes

entries.label: arrowroot
entries.definition: Arrowroot (Maranta arundinacea) is a tropical plant native to the Caribbean and Central/South America. It's a rhizome — an underground stem, similar in concept to ginger or turmeric. Arrowroot is most famous as a starch/thickener rather than a table vegetable.

entries.label: artichoke
entries.definition: The globe ARTICHOKE (Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus), also known as French artichoke and green artichoke in the USA, is a variety of a species of thistle cultivated as a food. Leaves are often removed one at a time, and the fleshy base eaten, with hollandaise, vinegar, butter, mayonnaise, aioli, lemon juice, or other sauces. The fibrous upper part of each leaf is usually discarded. The heart is

entries.label: Artichoke heart
entries.definition: The heart is eaten when the inedible choke has been peeled away from the base and discarded.

entries.label: asparagus
entries.definition: Asparagus, or garden asparagus, folk name sparrow grass, scientific name Asparagus officinalis is a spring vegetable, a flowering perennial plant species in the genus Asparagus;

entries.label: kanpyo
entries.definition: Kanpyo is a Japanese ingredient made from dried strips of gourd — specifically the flesh of the calabash or bottle gourd (a variety called yūgao, related to what's sometimes called "bottle gourd" or "calabash" in English). To make it, the gourd is peeled into long, thin ribbons, then sun-dried until they become firm, chewy strips. Before use, the dried strips are rehydrated and usually simmered in

entries.label: bitter melon
entries.definition: A balsam pear is another name for bitter melon (Momordica charantia), a tropical vine in the gourd family. It's widely grown across Asia, Africa, the Caribbean, and South America. True to both its names, it has a pronounced bitter taste — the most bitter of any commonly eaten vegetable.

entries.label: bamboo
entries.definition: The bamboos are evergreen perennial flowering plants in the subfamily Bambusoideae of the grass family Poaceae.

entries.label: bamboo shoot
entries.definition: Bamboo shoots or bamboo sprouts are the edible shoots (new bamboo culms that come out of the ground) of many bamboo species including Bambusa vulgaris and Phyllostachys edulis.

entries.label: sasa veitchii
entries.definition: large species of bamboo grass

entries.label: taro shoots
entries.definition: The young sprouts/suckers that grow off the main corm (sometimes called "huli" in Hawaiian), which are more often used for propagating new plants than eating, though tender young shoots can be cooked too.

entries.label: beetroot
entries.definition: BEETROOT is the taproot portion of the beet plant

entries.label: broccoli raab
entries.definition: Broccoli raab (also spelled rabe, and sometimes called rapini) is a leafy green vegetable popular in Italian and Mediterranean cooking. Despite its name, it's not closely related to regular broccoli — it's actually more closely related to turnips. It has long, thin stalks with dark green, slightly jagged leaves and small florets that resemble tiny broccoli heads. The whole plant is edible — leaves

entries.label: burdock root
entries.definition: Burdock root is an edible root vegetable and herbal remedy that comes from the burdock plant (Arctium lappa), a large-leafed plant native to northern Asia and Europe, now grown worldwide. it's especially popular in Japanese cuisine, where it's known as gobō. It has a mildly sweet, earthy flavor and a crunchy texture.

entries.label: celtuce
entries.definition: Celtuce (also called stem lettuce, celery lettuce, or Chinese lettuce) is a vegetable that's actually a cultivar of the same species as regular lettuce (Lactuca sativa), but it's grown specifically for its thick, edible stem rather than its leaves. The stem has a mild, slightly sweet, and nutty flavor with a crisp, crunchy texture — often compared to a cross between celery, cucumber, and asparagus

entries.label: fuki
entries.definition: Fuki (Petasites japonicus) is a flowering plant native to Europe and parts of Asia and North America. In Japanese cuisine, fuki is a well-established vegetable and has been eaten for centuries: The leaf stalks (petioles) are the main edible part — boiled, then peeled and used in simmered dishes (nimono), stir-fries, or as a side dish; The flower buds (fuki no tō) are a beloved spring delicacy, eat

entries.label: mustard cabbage
entries.definition: Mustard Cabbage (also called gai choy or Chinese mustard) is a leafy green vegetable common in Asian cuisine. Large, crinkled or smooth leaves, often with a pale green or yellowish color; can look somewhat like bok choy or napa cabbage. Distinctly pungent and slightly bitter, with a mustardy kick that mellows when cooked.

entries.label: heart of palm
entries.definition: The heart of palm is the inner core of certain palm trees, harvested as a vegetable and typically canned or jarred in brine.

entries.label: pokeberry shoots
entries.definition: Pokeberry (pokeweed, Phytolacca americana) shoots are a traditional Southern U.S. food, often called "poke sallet" or "poke salad." The plant is toxic, but very young shoots can be made edible through careful preparation.

entries.label: Welsh onion
entries.definition: Allium fistulosum, the Welsh onion, also commonly called bunching onion, long green onion, Japanese bunching onion, and spring onion, is a species of perennial plant. A. fistulosum is an ingredient in Asian cuisine, especially in East and Southeast Asia. In the West, A. fistulosum is primarily used as a scallion or salad onion.

entries.label: shallot
entries.definition: The SHALLOT is a type of onion, specifically a botanical variety of the species Allium cepa.

entries.label: leek
entries.definition: The LEEK is a vegetable, a cultivar of Allium ampeloprasum, the broadleaf wild leek. Leeks have a mild, onion-like taste. In its raw state, the vegetable is crunchy and firm. The edible portions of the leek are the white base of the leaves (above the roots and stem base), the light green parts, and to a lesser extent the dark green parts of the leaves. Leeks are typically chopped into slices 5–10

entries.label: tuber
entries.definition: A tuber is a swollen underground stem (or in some cases a swollen root), used for storing nutrients — like potatoes. It typically grows at the end of a rhizome or stolon, not as the plant's central root.

entries.label: eppaw
entries.definition: Eppaw is the edible tuber of the duck potato plant (Sagittaria latifolia, also called wapato or arrowhead), traditionally eaten by some Native American groups, particularly noted in Seminole/Florida contexts. It's a starchy, potato-like root vegetable that grows in shallow water and marshes, and was historically gathered as a wild food source.

entries.label: root vegetable
entries.definition: ROOT VEGETABLES are underground plant parts eaten by humans as food.

entries.label: starchy root vegetable
entries.definition: Root vegetable with a significant amount of starch.

entries.label: carrot
entries.definition: The CARROT (Daucus carota subsp. sativus) is a root vegetable, usually orange in colour, though purple, black, red, white, and yellow cultivars exist

entries.label: vegetable oyster
entries.definition: Root has pale tan or beige skin, with white flesh. Native to the Mediterranean; naturalized widely, including in North America, with the classic "oyster-like" flavor that gave it its common name.

entries.label: sweet potato
entries.definition: A sweet potato is a starchy root vegetable. It grows underground as a swollen root, It's skin can be orange, purple, white, or reddish; flesh is often orange, but also comes in white or purple. It has a naturally sweet flavor, especially when roasted or baked. It is rich in beta-carotene (converts to vitamin A) and a good source of fiber, vitamin C, potassium, and manganese, and has complex carboh

entries.label: tapioca
entries.definition: TAPIOCA is a starch extracted from cassava root (tapioca seems to be the same as tapioca starch, but not used as such on ingredient lists)

entries.label: dry tapioca pearls
entries.definition: Tapioca pearls are made from cassava root starch, a plant native to South America but now cultivated widely across Brazil, Southeast Asia, and Africa. On their own, dry pearls are essentially flavorless and starchy, taking on a mild sweetness and chewy, translucent texture once cooked. They're most commonly used in bubble tea, puddings, and Southeast Asian desserts, or as a thickener in soups and

entries.label: yam
entries.definition: Yam is the common name for some plant species in the genus Dioscorea (family Dioscoreaceae) that form edible tubers. In some places, other (unrelated) root vegetables are sometimes referred to as "yams".

entries.label: chinese yam
entries.definition: Japanese mountain yam is native to China and Japan. Unlike most yams, it's often eaten raw — grated, it becomes sticky and mucilaginous (called tororo in Japanese cooking), used as a topping for rice, soba, or mixed into batters. It can also be cooked (steamed, boiled, fried).

entries.label: potato
entries.definition: The POTATO is a starchy, tuberous crop from the perennial nightshade Solanum tuberosum.
