entries.label: tahitian taro
entries.definition: In Hawaii specifically, "Tahitian" is also a distinct named cultivar — it was introduced from Tahiti by horticulturist Gerrit Parmile Wilder.

entries.label: yambean
entries.definition: Yambean is a tropical legume (in the bean family, Fabaceae) grown primarily for its large, starchy, edible tuber/root. Native to Mexico and Central America, widely cultivated across Latin America and Southeast Asia. Mildly sweet, very crunchy, similar to a cross between an apple and a water chestnut — it stays crisp even when cooked.

entries.label: yautia
entries.definition: Yautia (also called malanga or taro coco) is a starchy root vegetable widely used in Latin American and Caribbean cuisine. Earthy, slightly nutty flavor, denser and less slimy than taro. When cooked, it becomes soft and starchy — similar to a potato but with more depth of flavor.

entries.label: crudités
entries.definition: Crudités (plural only) are traditional French appetizers consisting of sliced or whole raw vegetables[1] which are typically dipped in a vinaigrette or other dipping sauce. Examples of crudités include celery sticks, carrot sticks, cucumber sticks, bell pepper strips, broccoli, cauliflower, fennel, and asparagus spears.

entries.label: avocado
entries.definition: The AVOCADO (Persea americana) is a tree classified as a member of the flowering plant family Lauraceae. The fruit of the plant, also called an avocado, is botanically a large berry containing a single large seed.

entries.label: borage
entries.definition: Borage, also known as a starflower, is an annual herb in the flowering plant family Boraginaceae. It is native to the Mediterranean region. Borage is used as either a fresh vegetable or a dried herb.

entries.label: aloe vera
entries.definition: ALOE VERA is a succulent plant species of the genus Aloe.

entries.label: drumstick pods
entries.definition: "Drumstick" is the common name for the long, slender seed pods of the moringa tree (Moringa oleifera), sometimes called the horseradish tree or ben tree. They're a popular vegetable in South Asian, Southeast Asian, and African cuisines. Long, thin, ridged green pods, often 1–3 feet long. Mild, slightly sweet, a bit like asparagus or green beans.

entries.label: Konjac
entries.definition: Konjac is a common name of the East and Southeast Asian plant Amorphophallus konjac (syn. A. rivieri), which has an edible corm (bulbo-tuber).

entries.label: horseradish
entries.definition: HORSERADISH (Armoracia rusticana, syn. Cochlearia armoracia) is a perennial plant of the family Brassicaceae. The intact horseradish root has hardly any aroma. When cut or grated enzymes from the now-broken plant cells break down sinigrin (a glucosinolate) to produce allyl isothiocyanate (mustard oil), which irritates the mucous membranes of the sinuses and eyes. Grated mash should be used immedia

entries.label: Jerusalem artichoke
entries.definition: JERUSALEM ARTICHOKE (Helianthus tuberosus), also called sunroot, sunchoke, earth apple, or topinambour, is a species of sunflower. The tubers are sometimes used as a substitute for potatoes: they have a similar consistency, and in their raw form have a similar texture, but a sweeter, nuttier flavor; raw and sliced thinly, they are fit for a salad.

entries.label: parsnip
entries.definition: The PARSNIP (Pastinaca sativa) is a root vegetable closely related to the carrot and parsley.

entries.label: white icicle radish
entries.definition: White Icicle radish is a heirloom radish variety, notable for its long, slender white root. Milder and less peppery-hot than round red radishes, with a crisp, juicy bite.

entries.label: nopales
entries.definition: Nopales are the edible pads (paddles) of the prickly pear cactus (genus Opuntia), widely used in Mexican cuisine. Slightly tart and grassy, a bit like green beans or okra, with a similar mucilaginous (slightly slimy) texture when cooked, especially if simmered.

entries.label: thistle
entries.definition: Thistle is the popular name of a group of flowering plants characterised by leaves with sharp spikes on the margins, mostly in the family Asteraceae. (Wikipedia)

entries.label: bell pepper
entries.definition: The bell pepper (also known as sweet pepper, pepper or capsicum /ˈkæpsɪkəm/) is a cultivar group of the species Capsicum annuum. Cultivars of the plant produce fruits in different colours, including red, yellow, orange, green, white, and purple.

entries.label: chili pepper
entries.definition: El chile, ají o guindilla, es una variedad de pimiento picante. Es el fruto (baya) de diversas especies de plantas del género Capsicum.

entries.label: ancho peppers
entries.definition: Ancho peppers are the dried form of the poblano pepper. Sweet and fruity with notes of raisin, dried plum, and a mild smokiness — sometimes with a hint of coffee or tobacco. It's considered one of the more complex, dessert-like tasting dried chiles.

entries.label: banana pepper
entries.definition: Banana peppers are a mild, tangy pepper named for their curved, elongated shape and pale yellow color — closely resembling a banana. Tangy and slightly sweet with a mild vinegary bite, especially when pickled — very different from the "grassy" heat of a jalapeño.

entries.label: hungarian peppers
entries.definition: Hungarian peppers usually refers to a family of peppers most associated with Hungarian cuisine and paprika production. Tangy, slightly sweet, with a crisp bite — similar in style to a banana pepper but noticeably spicier.

entries.label: serrano peppers
entries.definition: Serrano peppers are a type of chili pepper originating from the mountainous regions of Puebla and Hidalgo in Mexico. They have a bright, crisp, and grassy with a clean heat — often described as sharper and more straightforward than jalapeño.

entries.label: pasilla peppers
entries.definition: A Mexican chili. The fresh version of this pepper is actually called chilaca. Once dried, it becomes "pasilla" — long, slender, and dark brownish-black with a raisin-like, wrinkled texture. Rich, deep, and slightly fruity with notes of raisin, dried cherry, and mild chocolate/tobacco undertones — a favorite for building complex sauces.

entries.label: Espelette chili pepper
entries.definition: The Espelette pepper is a variety of Capsicum annuum that is cultivated in the French commune of Espelette, Pyrénées-Atlantiques, traditionally the northern territory of the Basque people. On 1 June 2000, it was classified as an AOC product and was confirmed as an APO product on 22 August 2002.

entries.label: jalapeno pepper
entries.definition: Jalapeño peppers are probably the most familiar chili in American and Mexican cooking — a good middle-ground pepper for both flavor and heat. The taste is grassy, slightly sweet, and vegetal with a clean, building heat.

entries.label: allspice
entries.definition: ALLSPICE, also known as Jamaica pepper, myrtle pepper, pimenta, or pimento, is the dried unripe berry of Pimenta dioica, a midcanopy tree native to the Greater Antilles, southern Mexico, and Central America, now cultivated in many warm parts of the world.

entries.label: Sichuan pepper
entries.definition: Sichuan pepper is a spice made from the dried pericarp (outer shell of the fruit) of a plant of the genus Zanthoxylum in the family Rutaceae. (Wikipedia)

entries.label: tomatillo
entries.definition: Tomatillos are small, round fruits (botanically fruits, culinarily treated as vegetables) that look like little green tomatoes wrapped in a papery husk. They're a staple in Mexican cooking, especially for salsa verde. Tart, tangy, and slightly citrusy — quite different from a regular tomato. Raw ones are firm and sour; cooking mellows and sweetens them a bit.

entries.label: sundried tomatoes
entries.definition: Sun-dried tomatoes are ripe tomatoes that lose most of their water content after spending a majority of their drying time in the sun.

entries.definition: The TURNIP (Brassica rapa subsp. rapa) is a root vegetable commonly grown in temperate climates worldwide for its white, fleshy taproot.

entries.label: water chestnut
entries.definition: Eleocharis dulcis, the Chinese water chestnut or water chestnut, is a grass-like sedge. It is grown in many countries for its edible corms.

entries.label: pumpkin
entries.definition: A PUMPKIN is a cultivar of a squash plant, most commonly of Cucurbita pepo, that is round, with smooth, slightly ribbed skin, and deep yellow to orange coloration.

entries.label: white-flowered gourd
entries.definition: "White-flowered gourd" (calabash) refers to Lagenaria siceraria — also known as bottle gourd, calabash gourd, opo squash, or long melon. It's the same plant whose hard-shelled fruits are dried and used as bottles, bowls, or musical instruments, but when eaten as food it's harvested young and tender, before the shell hardens. Very mild, slightly sweet, with a texture similar to zucchini or chayote

entries.label: dishcloth
entries.definition: "Dishcloth gourd" (also called towel gourd, sponge gourd, or luffa) is the common name for Luffa — usually Luffa aegyptiaca (smooth luffa) or Luffa acutangula (angled/ridged luffa, sometimes called "Chinese okra"). It's a tropical vine in the cucumber/squash family, common in Asian, African, and some Mediterranean cuisines. The flesh is mild, slightly sweet, and a bit like a cross between zucchini

entries.label: red kuri squash
entries.definition: Red kuri squash (often spelled 'kari') (katakana:ウチキクリ) is thin skinned orange colored winter squash, that has the appearance of a small pumpkin without the ridges.

entries.label: turnip rape
entries.definition: Turnip rape (Brassica rapa subsp. oleifera, also called field mustard or rybs in some regions) is grown for its seeds, which are pressed for oil. It's one of the plants used to produce canola oil (along with rapeseed, Brassica napus). Young leaves of turnip rape can be eaten as leafy greens, similar to mustard greens or other brassica greens, in some regional cuisines.

entries.label: beans
entries.definition: A BEAN is a seed of one of several genera of the flowering plant family Fabaceae, which are used for human or animal food.

entries.label: flat bean
entries.definition: FLAT BEANS, also known as helda beans, romano beans and "gavar fhali" in some Indian states, are a variety of Phaseolus coccineus, known as runner bean with edible pods that have a characteristic wide and flat shape.

entries.label: winged beans
entries.definition: Winged beans (Psophocarpus tetragonolobus) are a tropical legume known for their distinctive four-sided, ruffled or "winged" pods — the edges look like jagged ribbons running down the length of each pod. Almost the entire plant is edible: pods, seeds, leaves, flowers, and even the tuberous roots can all be eaten. That's unusual among legumes. High in protein: the seeds in particular are very prote

entries.label: yardlong beans
entries.definition: Yardlong beans (also called Chinese long beans, snake beans, or asparagus beans) are a type of legume known for their dramatically long, slender pods — typically 12 to 30 inches long, though they're usually picked and sold around 18 inches. They have a slightly nuttier, more savory flavor than regular green beans, with a denser, chewier texture that holds up well to high-heat cooking like stir-fry

entries.label: legume
entries.definition: A LEGUME is a plant in the family Fabaceae (or Leguminosae), or the fruit or seed of such a plant (also called a pulse). Legumes are grown agriculturally, primarily for human consumption. Grain legumes include beans, lentils, lupins, peas, and peanuts.

entries.label: pulse
entries.definition: pulse = just the dry, harvested seed of specific legume crops. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) recognizes 11 categories of pulses: Dry beans — includes kidney beans, navy beans, pinto beans, black beans, lima beans, mung beans, adzuki beans; Dry broad beans — fava beans, horse beans, broad beans (in dried form); Dry peas — includes split peas, whole dried peas (green or yellow); Chi

entries.label: hyacinth bean
entries.definition: Hyacinth beans (Lablab purpureus, also called lablab beans, dolichos beans, or Egyptian beans) are a fast-growing climbing vine grown both as an ornamental plant and a food crop. The young, immature pods can be cooked and eaten like green beans. However, the mature beans and pods contain cyanogenic glycosides and must be thoroughly cooked (usually boiled with water changes) before eating — they're

entries.label: lima bean
entries.definition: Phaseolus lunatus, commonly known as the LIMA BEAN, butter bean, sieva bean, Double Bean or Madagascar bean, is a legume grown for its edible seeds or beans

entries.label: red bean
entries.definition: Red Rajmah (red kidney beans) originates from the Andean region of Central and South America, from where it spread worldwide and became deeply rooted in South Asian cuisine, especially in Punjabi and North Indian cooking. It has a glossy deep-red skin with a soft, creamy interior and a rich, slightly sweet, earthy flavor. Most famously simmered into the classic "rajma" curry with tomatoes, onions,

entries.label: brown kidney bean
entries.definition: Brown Rajmah (brown kidney beans) traces its origins to the Andean highlands of the Americas, from where it spread globally and became widely cultivated across South Asia, especially in Kashmir and northern India. It has a light tan-brown skin with a mild, nutty, slightly earthy flavor and a firmer texture than red or black varieties. Commonly simmered in spiced curries, added to soups, stews, sal

entries.label: black kidney bean
entries.definition: Black Rajmah (black kidney beans) originates from the Andean region of Central and South America, later becoming a staple across South Asia, particularly in North Indian and Kashmiri cuisine. Distinct from the more common red rajmah, it has a deep black-maroon skin and a dense, creamy interior with an earthy, slightly sweet flavor. It's typically slow-cooked in a thick, spiced tomato-onion gravy,

entries.label: horse gram
entries.definition: Native to South Asia, horse gram is an ancient, drought-resistant legume long cultivated across India, Nepal, and parts of Africa and Southeast Asia, where it's also used as livestock fodder. Small, flattish, and reddish-brown, it has a robust, earthy, slightly nutty flavor with a firm bite. Traditionally simmered into soups, stews, and sprouted dishes, or ground into flour, it's especially prized

entries.label: mung bean
entries.definition: Green gram, whole (Vigna radiata), commonly known as mung bean or moong, originated in the Indian subcontinent and spread across Asia and beyond through centuries of trade and cultivation. Sold whole with its green skin intact, it has a mild, slightly sweet, earthy flavor and a firm texture that softens on cooking. It's used worldwide in soups, stews, curries, salads, and sprouts, and is especiall

entries.definition: Hulled and split black gram. Hulling removes the black skin which gives it a white color.

entries.label: borlotti bean
entries.definition: The borlotti bean is a variety of common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) first bred in Colombia as the cargamanto.

entries.label: lupin bean
entries.definition: Lupin or lupini beans are the yellow legume seeds of the genus Lupinus. They are traditionally eaten as a pickled snack food. The lupin is devoid of starch, which is very unusual for a species of edible bean. Lupin allergy may cause life-threatening anaphylaxis in sensitive individuals. Only "sweet" varieties of lupin are used for human food

entries.label: moth bean
entries.definition: Moth beans (Vigna aconitifolia), also called mat beans or matki, originated in the Indian subcontinent, where they've been cultivated for centuries as a hardy, drought-resistant crop suited to arid regions. Small, olive-brown, and oblong, they carry an earthy, slightly nutty flavor with a firm bite once cooked. Across South Asia, they're prepared whole or sprouted—simmered into curries, stewed wit

entries.label: broad bean
entries.definition: Vicia faba, also known in the culinary sense as the broad bean, fava bean, or faba bean is a species of flowering plant in the pea and bean family Fabaceae.

entries.label: Sweet bean paste
entries.definition: Sweet bean paste is used throughout East Asian cuisine, primarily as a filling for sweet desserts and pastries.

entries.label: cowpea
entries.definition: Cowpeas (Vigna unguiculata), also known as black-eyed peas or southern peas, originated in West Africa thousands of years ago before spreading to the Mediterranean, Asia, and the Americas via trade and slavery routes. They have an earthy, mildly nutty flavor with a creamy texture once cooked. Versatile in the kitchen, they're used in stews, salads, fritters (like akara), rice dishes (such as Hoppi

entries.label: pea
entries.definition: Peas are a good example of how the same plant can fall into different categories depending on how it's harvested and used. Fresh peas (green peas, snap peas, snow peas) are harvested young and eaten fresh, in or out of the pod. they are classified as a vegetable, not a pulse. Dried peas are the same plant, but the peas are left to mature and dry on the vine before harvesting. This is what counts a

entries.label: pigeon pea
entries.definition: Pigeon peas (Cajanus cajan) differ quite a bit depending on whether they're picked green or left to dry on the plant. The green peas have a mild, slightly sweet flavor; the dried peas have Earthier, nuttier flavor — closer to lentils or other dried pulses

entries.label: Rice bean
entries.definition: Rice beans (Vigna umbellata) are a small, oval legume native to South and Southeast Asia, widely cultivated in northeast India, Nepal, Bhutan, southern China, Indonesia, and Thailand. They have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor and a texture similar to mung beans, cooking relatively quickly compared to other pulses. Across their growing regions, rice beans are used in soups, stews, curries, sal

entries.label: chickpea
entries.definition: Chickpeas (Cicer arietinum), also known as garbanzo beans, are one of the world's oldest cultivated legumes, originating in the Middle East over 7,000 years ago and now grown widely across the Mediterranean, India, and the Americas. They have a mild, slightly nutty, earthy flavor with a firm yet creamy texture once cooked, making them extremely versatile in the kitchen. Chickpeas star in dishes li

entries.label: edible-podded pea
entries.definition: The edible-podded pea (Pisum sativum var. saccharatum) are a variety of pea eaten whole in its pod while still unripe.

entries.label: snow pea
entries.definition: Snow peas (mangetout) — flat pods with small, barely-developed seeds inside.

entries.label: sugar snap peas
entries.definition: Sugar snap peas — plumper, rounder pods (than mangetout) with full-size seeds, but the pod stays tender and edible

entries.label: split pea
entries.definition: Split peas are dried, peeled, and halved seeds of Pisum sativum, a legume cultivated for millennia across Europe, Central Asia, and the Indian subcontinent. Available in yellow and green varieties, they have an earthy, slightly sweet, nutty flavor that deepens with cooking. Widely used worldwide — in Dutch erwtensoep, Indian dal, British pease pudding, Middle Eastern stews, and American split pea

entries.label: lentils
entries.definition: Originating in the Fertile Crescent over 8,000 years ago, lentils spread across the Mediterranean, Middle East, South Asia, and beyond, becoming a dietary cornerstone worldwide. Known as "dal" in South Asia, they come in many varieties—red, green, brown, black, yellow—each with subtly different flavor, from mild and sweet to earthy. Quick-cooking and hulling-friendly, lentils are simmered into sou

entries.label: almond
entries.definition: The almond (Prunus amygdalus, syn. Prunus dulcis) is a species of tree native to Iran and surrounding countries, but widely cultivated elsewhere. The almond is also the name of the edible and widely cultivated seed of this tree.

entries.label: beechnut
entries.definition: Beechnuts are the small, triangular nuts produced by beech trees (genus Fagus), particularly the American beech (Fagus grandifolia) and European beech (Fagus sylvatica). They're edible for humans in moderate amounts, but raw beechnuts contain a compound called fagin (sometimes also referenced as related tannins) that can cause mild digestive upset or headaches if eaten in large quantities. Roastin

entries.label: brazil nut
entries.definition: The Brazil nut (Bertholletia excelsa) is a South American tree in the family Lecythidaceae, and it is also the name of the tree's commercially harvested edible seeds.

entries.label: white walnut
entries.definition: Butternuts (Juglans cinerea), also called white walnuts, are a species of walnut tree native to eastern North America. The nutmeats are eaten and used in baking.

entries.label: chestnut
entries.definition: The chestnuts are a group of eight or nine species of deciduous trees and shrubs in the genus Castanea. The name also refers to the edible nuts they produce. The sweet chestnut produces an edible seed, the chestnut, which has been used in cooking since ancient times.

entries.label: hazelnut
entries.definition: The HAZELNUT is the nut of the hazel and therefore includes any of the nuts deriving from species of the genus Corylus, especially the nuts of the species Corylus avellana.

entries.label: hickorynut
entries.definition: A hickory nut is the edible nut produced by trees in the genus Carya — the same genus that includes pecans. They're native mostly to North America, with a few species in Asia. Encased in a thick, husk-like outer covering that splits open (fully or partially, depending on species) when ripe, revealing a hard shell. Inside that shell is the actual nutmeat. Flavor varies a lot by species — some, like

entries.label: macadamia nut
entries.definition: La noix de macadamia, ou noix du Queensland est le fruit du noyer du Queensland.

entries.label: spanish peanut
entries.definition: Spanish peanuts are a specific variety of peanut, distinct from the more common runner or Virginia types you'd find as standard roasted peanuts or in most peanut butter. Grown mainly in Oklahoma and Texas in the US, though the name comes from their origin.

entries.label: pecan nut
entries.definition: La noix de pécan ou pacane est le fruit du pacanier (Carya illinoinensis), arbre de la famille des Juglandacées.

entries.label: pilinut
entries.definition: A pili nut (Canarium ovatum) is a tropical tree nut native to the Philippines, particularly grown in the Bicol region. The nut has a rich, buttery flavor and texture, often compared to a cross between an almond and a macadamia nut — but generally considered even richer and more delicate. They're eaten raw, roasted, or candied, and are also used in pastries, pesto-style sauces, and as a snack food.

entries.label: walnut
entries.definition: A walnut is the nut of any tree of the genus Juglans. After full ripening for its edible seed when the shell has been discarded, it is used as a garnish or a snack.

entries.label: aniseed
entries.definition: Anise, also called aniseed, is a flowering plant in the family Apiaceae. It is widely cultivated and used to flavor food and alcoholic drinks, especially around the Mediterranean.

entries.label: breadnut tree seeds
entries.definition: Breadnut (also called kamansi in the Philippines, or "chataigne" in the Caribbean) produces large, spiky green fruits similar in appearance to breadfruit, but unlike the common seedless breadfruit variety, breadnut fruits are packed with edible seeds — usually 100+ per fruit. The seeds themselves are roughly the size of chestnuts or large beans. Typically boiled, roasted, or steamed before eating.

entries.label: chia
entries.definition: SALVIA HISPANICA, commonly known as CHIA, is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae

entries.label: chia seed
entries.definition: Native to Mexico and Guatemala, chia seeds come from the flowering plant Salvia hispanica. Black seeds are the traditional, more widely available variety; white seeds are a naturally occurring lighter variant, often prized for their appearance in pale-colored dishes. Both share a mild, nutty flavor and neutral taste, absorbing surrounding flavors easily. When soaked, they develop a gel-like textur

entries.label: cottonseed
entries.definition: Cottonseed is the seed of the cotton plant (genus Gossypium), harvested as a byproduct of cotton fiber production. After cotton bolls are picked, the fluffy fiber (lint) is separated from the seeds during a process called ginning. Each cotton boll contains several seeds embedded in the fiber. Raw cottonseed contains a natural compound called gossypol, which is toxic to humans in significant quanti

entries.label: flax seed
entries.definition: Flax, also known as common flax or linseed, is a flowering plant, Linum usitatissimum, in the family Linaceae. Flax seeds occur in two basic varieties/colors: brown or yellow (golden linseeds).

entries.label: lotus seed
entries.definition: Lotus seeds are the edible seeds of the lotus plant (Nelumbo nucifera), an aquatic plant grown widely across Asia, particularly in China, India, and Southeast Asia. Fresh seeds have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor and a crisp texture, often eaten raw or lightly cooked. Dried seeds are used in soups, congee, and herbal tonics

entries.label: poppyseed
entries.definition: The seed of the poppy.

entries.label: safflower seed kernels
entries.definition: Safflower seed kernels are the inner, edible part of the seeds from the safflower plant (Carthamus tinctorius), an oilseed crop in the daisy/thistle family that's related to sunflowers. Safflower kernels are quite high in fat (mostly unsaturated, especially linoleic acid — an omega-6 fatty acid), along with protein and fiber. They're also a source of vitamin E and various minerals.

entries.label: tahini
entries.definition: Tahini is a condiment made from toasted ground hulled sesame.

entries.label: pepper
entries.definition: Peppercorns and the ground pepper derived from them may be described simply as pepper, or more precisely as black pepper (cooked and dried unripe fruit), green pepper (dried unripe fruit), and white pepper (ripe fruit seeds).

entries.label: miso
entries.definition: MISO is a traditional Japanese seasoning produced by fermenting soybeans with salt and kōji (the fungus Aspergillus oryzae) and sometimes rice, barley, seaweed or other ingredients.

entries.label: plantes aromatiques et épices dont herbes aromatiques

aliases.text: plantes aromatiques et épices dont herbes aromatiques
aliases.norm: plantes aromatiques et épices dont herbes aromatiques

entries.label: asafoetida
entries.definition: A resinous gum from the stem and roots of Ferula species such as Ferula foetida and Ferula assa-foetida, having a strong, unpleasant smell, with culinary and medical uses

entries.label: caraway
entries.definition: CARAWAY (Carum carvi), is a biennial plant in the family Apiaceae. The fruits, usually used whole, have a pungent, anise-like flavor. Caraway is used as a spice in breads, especially rye bread. Caraway is also used in desserts, liquors, casseroles, and other foods.

entries.label: cayenne pepper
entries.definition: The CAYENNE PEPPER is a type of Capsicum annuum. It is usually a moderately hot chili pepper used to flavor dishes.

entries.label: chili powder
entries.definition: In the USDA FoodData Central database, chili powder is a seasoning blend, not a single-ingredient spice. It's typically listed as a blend of ground dried chili peppers combined with other spices — commonly cumin, oregano, garlic powder, onion powder, and salt, though blends vary by brand and recipe.

entries.label: curry powder
entries.definition: CURRY POWDER is a spice mix originating from the Indian subcontinent.

entries.label: curry paste
entries.definition: CURRY PASTE usually refers to a paste used as a cooking ingredient in the preparation of a curry.

entries.label: turmeric
entries.definition: TURMERIC is a flowering plant of the ginger family, Zingiberaceae, the roots of which are used in cooking. Note that turmeric contains some curcumine (E100).

entries.label: nutmeg
entries.definition: NUTMEG is the seed or ground spice of several species of the genus Myristica.

entries.label: cassia
entries.definition: Cinnamomum cassia, called Chinese cassia or Chinese cinnamon, is an evergreen tree originating in southern China

entries.label: ceylon cinnamon
entries.definition: CINNAMOMUM VERUM, called true cinnamon tree or Ceylon cinnamon tree is a small evergreen tree belonging to the family Lauraceae, native to Sri Lanka.

entries.label: clove
entries.definition: CLOVEs are the aromatic flower buds of a tree in the family Myrtaceae, Syzygium aromaticum.

entries.label: ginger
entries.definition: GINGER (Zingiber officinale) is a flowering plant whose rhizome, ginger root or simply ginger, is widely used as a spice or a folk medicine

entries.label: mustard
entries.definition: Powder or paste made from seeds of the mustard plant, and used as a condiment or a spice.

entries.label: mustard seed
entries.definition: A small, round seed of the mustard plant.

entries.label: dijon mustard
entries.definition: A kind of mustard made with verjuice (or, more recently, white wine) instead of vinegar.

entries.label: pink peppercorn
entries.definition: A PINK PEPPERCORN is a dried berry of the shrub Schinus molle, commonly known as the Peruvian peppertree. Although a peppercorn is the dried fruit of a plant from the genus Piper, pink peppercorns came to be called such because they resemble peppercorns, and because they, too, have a peppery flavour. As they are members of the cashew family, they may cause allergic reactions including anaphylaxis

entries.label: dill
entries.definition: dill (anethum graveolens) is an annual herb in the celery family apiaceae. dill is widely grown in eurasia where its leaves and seeds are used as a herb or spice for flavouring food.

entries.label: epazote
entries.definition: Epazote (Dysphania ambrosioides, formerly Chenopodium ambrosioides) is a pungent, aromatic herb widely used in Mexican and Central American cooking. The flavor is hard to pin down — people describe it as a mix of citrus, mint, anise, tar, and even petroleum-like notes. It's strong, so it's used in moderation, usually just a sprig or a few leaves per dish, added toward the end of cooking to preserv

entries.label: tarragon
entries.definition: TARRAGON (Artemisia dracunculus), is a species of perennial herb in the sunflower family. Tarragon is one of the four fines herbes of French cooking, and is particularly suitable for chicken, fish, and egg dishes.

entries.label: thyme
entries.definition: THYME is an aromatic perennial evergreen herb with culinary, medicinal, and ornamental uses. The most common variety is Thymus vulgaris.

entries.label: marjoram
entries.definition: Marjoram (Origanum majorana) is a somewhat cold-sensitive perennial herb or undershrub with sweet pine and citrus flavors.

entries.label: oregano
entries.definition: Oregano (Origanum vulgare) is a flowering plant in the mint family (Lamiaceae).

entries.label: coriander
entries.definition: Coriander (Coriandrum sativum), also known as cilantro or Chinese parsley, is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae.

entries.label: juniper
entries.definition: JUNIPERS are coniferous plants in the genus Juniperus of the cypress family Cupressaceae. Juniper berries are a spice used in a wide variety of culinary dishes and best known for the primary flavoring in gin. Juniper berry sauce is often a popular flavoring choice for quail, pheasant, veal, rabbit, venison and other game dishes.

entries.label: juniper berry
entries.definition: A JUNIPER BERRY is the female seed cone produced by the various species of junipers. Juniper berries are used in northern European and particularly Scandinavian cuisine to "impart a sharp, clear flavor" to meat dishes. Besides Norwegian and Swedish dishes, juniper berries are also sometimes used in German, Austrian, Czech, Polish and Hungarian cuisine, often with roasts (such as German sauerbraten

entries.label: liquorice
entries.definition: LIQUORICE or licorice is the root of Glycyrrhiza glabra from which a sweet flavour can be extracted.

entries.label: mate
entries.definition: Mate is a traditional South American caffeine-rich infused drink. It is prepared by steeping dried leaves of yerba mate in hot water and is served with a metal straw from a shared hollow calabash gourd

entries.label: psyllium
entries.definition: Psyllium is the seed husk of Plantago ovata, a plant part grown mainly in India (the world's dominant producer), with smaller output in Pakistan, Iran, and parts of Europe. Seeds are harvested and cleaned, then the husk is mechanically separated by milling and sifting, and sometimes ground into powder, without extraction or chemical treatment. It is nearly tasteless, with a slightly mucilaginous t

entries.label: purple coneflower
entries.definition: Native to the prairies and open woodlands of central and eastern North America, purple coneflower has long been used by Indigenous peoples before spreading globally as a cultivated herb. Today it's grown commercially across North America, Europe, and parts of Asia, with roots, leaves, and flowers harvested, dried, and processed into powders, extracts, teas, or tinctures. Its flavor is earthy, slig

aliases.text: concentrado de cártamo con efecto colorante
aliases.norm: concentrado de cártamo con efecto colorante

entries.label: sesbania flower
entries.definition: The flowers come from Sesbania grandiflora, a fast-growing tropical tree also called the vegetable hummingbird, hummingbird tree, or agati. It's a popular edible flower across South and Southeast Asian cuisines. Before cooking, the bitter stamens and pistil inside each flower are usually pinched out, leaving the sweeter petals. They taste mildly sweet and slightly bitter, with a delicate, slightly

entries.label: wasabi
entries.definition: WASABI (Eutrema japonicum or Wasabia japonica) or Japanese horseradish is a plant of the Brassicaceae family.

entries.label: Ashitaba
entries.definition: species of flowering plant in the carrot family

entries.label: chlorella
entries.definition: CHLORELLA is a genus of single-celled green algae belonging to the division Chlorophyta.

entries.label: spirulina
entries.definition: Spirulina is a blue-green algae (cyanobacterium) that's grown and processed as a food and dietary supplement. Very high in protein (roughly 55–70% by dry weight), including all essential amino acids. Rich in B vitamins (especially B12-like compounds, though its B12 isn't well-absorbed by humans), iron, and antioxidants like phycocyanin (the pigment giving it its blue-green color). It contains omeg

entries.label: seaweed
entries.definition: SEAWEED or macroalgae refers to several species of macroscopic, multicellular, marine algae.

entries.label: dulse
entries.definition: Palmaria palmata, also called dulse, dillisk or dilsk (from Irish/Scottish Gaelic duileasc/duileasg), red dulse, sea lettuce flakes, or creathnach, is a red alga (Rhodophyta) previously referred to as Rhodymenia palmata.

entries.label: Fucus
entries.definition: Fucus is a genus of brown algae found in the intertidal zones of rocky seashores almost throughout the world.

entries.label: glasswort
entries.definition: Salicornia is a genus of succulent, halophyte (salt tolerant) flowering plants in the family Amaranthaceae that grow in salt marshes, on beaches, and among mangroves. The main European species is often eaten and the main North American species is occasionally sold in grocery stores or appears on restaurant menus, usually as 'sea beans' or samphire greens or sea asparagus.

entries.label: tsunomata
entries.definition: Tsunomata (角叉, or つのまた) is the Japanese name for a type of red algae/seaweed. In Japanese cooking, it's traditionally soaked and used in salads, soups, or as a crunchy/chewy garnish. It has a mild, subtle sea flavor rather than a strong "seaweed" taste.

entries.label: laver
entries.definition: Laver is a type of edible seaweed — specifically a red algae from the genus Porphyra (and related species like Pyropia). It grows on rocks in intertidal zones along coastlines, particularly in the UK, Ireland, Japan, Korea, and other coastal regions. It has a savory, briny, slightly mineral taste — often described as umami-rich, similar to other seaweeds.

entries.label: nori
entries.definition: Nori (海苔) is the Japanese name for edible seaweed (a "sea vegetable") species of the red algae genus Pyropia, including P. yezoensis and P. tenera.

entries.label: sea lettuce
entries.definition: The sea lettuces comprise the genus Ulva, a group of edible green algae that is widely distributed along the coasts of the world's oceans.

entries.label: broadleaf sea lettuce
entries.definition: Sea lettuce (Ulva lactuca and related Ulva species) is a bright green marine macroalga found in coastal waters worldwide, thriving in nutrient-rich shallows from the Atlantic and Pacific to the Mediterranean. It is harvested wild from rocky shores and increasingly cultivated in tanks, ponds, or ropes at sea, then washed, dried, or freeze-dried and milled. Its taste is mildly salty, fresh, and slig

entries.label: thongweed
entries.definition: HIMANTHALIA ELONGATA is a brown alga (class Phaeophyta or Phaeophyceae) in the order Fucales, also known by the common names thongweed, sea thong and sea spaghetti.

entries.label: kelp
entries.definition: Kelp is a type of large brown seaweed that grows in cold, nutrient-rich coastal waters, and it's become a fairly common food ingredient, especially in East Asian cuisines. Kelp is notably rich in iodine, along with other minerals like calcium, magnesium, and iron. It's low in calories and contains some fiber. It has a natural savory, oceanic taste often described as umami. Kelp is a common term co

entries.label: kombu
entries.definition: KOMBU (from Japanese: 昆布, translit. konbu) is edible kelp from mostly the family Laminariaceae and is widely eaten in East Asia. There are about eighteen edible species in Laminariaceae and most of them, but not all, are called kombu.

entries.label: Saccharina japonica
entries.definition: Saccharina japonica is a marine species of the Phaeophyceae (brown algae) plant , a type of kelp or seaweed, that is extensively cultivated on ropes between the seas of Japan and Korea.[

entries.label: wakame
entries.definition: Wakame (ワカメ), UNDARIA PINNATIFIDA, is a species of edible seaweed, a type of marine algae, and a sea vegetable.

entries.label: Irish moss
entries.definition: Irish moss (Chondrus crispus), also called sea moss, is a red seaweed that grows along rocky Atlantic coastlines, especially around Ireland and the Caribbean. In food, it's valued mainly for the natural gelling and thickening properties it gets from carrageenan, a compound extracted from its cell walls. It has a mild, slightly salty or neutral taste on its own, so it's usually blended into other f

entries.label: golden chanterelle
entries.definition: CANTHARELLUS CIBARIUS is a species of golden chanterelle mushroom in the genus Cantharellus.

entries.label: cep
entries.definition: BOLETUS EDULIS (English:penny bun, cep, porcino or porcini) is a basidiomycete fungus, and the type species of the genus Boletus.

entries.label: Leccinum
entries.definition: LECCINUM is a genus of mushrooms from the Boletaceae family

entries.label: Imleria
entries.definition: IMLERIA is a genus of mushrooms from the Boletaceae family

entries.label: champignon
entries.definition: AGARICUS BISPORUS is an edible basidiomycete mushroom native to grasslands in Europe and North America.

entries.label: portobello
entries.definition: Agaricus bisporus is a single species that's sold under several names depending on maturity and color strain: white button mushrooms (young, white variety), crimini/baby bella (young, brown variety), and portobello (mature, brown variety, large cap). So "white mushrooms" specifically denotes the white cultivar picked at an early stage.

entries.label: button mushroom
entries.definition: Button mushroom and white mushroom both refer to young Agaricus bisporus, harvested early before the cap opens up. "Button" describes the shape/size (small, round, unopened cap), while "white" describes the color strain.

entries.label: milkcap
entries.definition: LACTARIUS is a genus of mushroom-producing, ectomycorrhizal fungi, containing several edible species.

entries.label: Enoki mushrooms
entries.definition: Enoki mushrooms (also called enokitake, golden needle mushrooms, or velvet shank) are a type of edible mushroom (Flammulina velutipes or filiformis) commonly used in East Asian cuisine, especially Japanese, Korean, and Chinese cooking. Mild, slightly sweet, and faintly fruity flavor; crisp, crunchy texture, even after cooking; Often described as having a delicate, almost noodle-like quality

entries.label: pepeao
entries.definition: Fresh pepeiao has a convex shape with a smooth, sometimes wrinkly surface, and can be a purply gray-brown color. It has a slightly chewy texture that many describe as rubbery-crunchy. It grows wild on logs of koa and kukui trees in Hawaii, typically on fallen or dying tree branches, often appearing after rain. It's known for its ability to absorb flavors when cooked and is commonly added to soups

entries.label: maitake mushroom
entries.definition: Maitake mushrooms (Grifola frondosa) are a type of edible mushroom native to Japan, China, and North America, where they grow wild at the base of oak, maple, and elm trees. Earthy, rich, and savory, often described as woodsy with a slightly peppery note. They have a nice meaty texture when cooked, similar to other polypore mushrooms. Popular in Japanese and other Asian cuisines — sautéed, roasted,

entries.label: chestnut mushroom
entries.definition: The mushroom commonly sold as "chestnut mushroom" is typically Pholiota adiposa (sometimes marketed varieties are hybrids/cultivars developed for the table), native to East Asia and popularized by Japanese cultivators.

entries.label: shiitake
entries.definition: The SHIITAKE (Lentinula edodes) is an edible mushroom native to East Asia, which is cultivated and consumed in many Asian countries.

entries.label: oyster mushroom
entries.definition: PLEUROTUS OSTREATUS, the oyster mushroom, is a common edible mushroom.

entries.label: wood ear
entries.definition: "Cloud ear" (also called wood ear, black fungus, or mù'ěr 木耳 in Chinese) refers to mushrooms in the genus Auricularia — most commonly Auricularia auricula-judae or Auricularia cornea. They're a type of jelly fungus that grows on decaying or living wood, especially elder, beech, and other broadleaf trees. Cloud ears are prized more for their texture than flavor — they're crunchy, slightly gelatinou

entries.label: pepeiao
entries.definition: "Pepeao" is a Hawaiian word — it literally means "ear," and it's used in Hawaii to refer to a type of jelly fungus (wood ear mushroom, genus Auricularia) because of its ear-shaped, rubbery cap. It grows on dead or decaying wood and is edible, often used in soups and stir-fries, similar to how "wood ear" or "cloud ear" mushrooms are used in Chinese cuisine.

entries.label: truffle
entries.definition: A TRUFFLE is the fruiting body of a subterranean ascomycete fungus, predominantly one of the many species of the genus Tuber. In addition to Tuber, many other genera of fungi are classified as truffles including Geopora, Peziza, Choiromyces, Leucangium, and over a hundred others.

entries.label: Mortierella alpina oil
entries.definition: Mortierella alpina oil is derived from a soil-dwelling filamentous fungus, first isolated and studied for its lipid content in various regions worldwide, including Japan, China, and Europe, where it is produced industrially through fermentation. The refined oil is essentially flavorless and odorless, making it unobtrusive when blended into other products. It is primarily used as an additive in inf

entries.label: Quorn mushroom product
entries.definition: QUORN is a meat substitute product originating in the UK and sold primarily in Europe, but also available in 19 countries.

entries.label: fish
entries.definition: Fish are gill-bearing aquatic craniate animals that lack limbs with digits.

entries.label: flat fish
entries.definition: Flat fish are a group of fish that live and swim mostly on the ocean floor, and their most striking feature is that their bodies are flattened sideways (laterally compressed) so they end up lying and swimming on one side rather than upright.

entries.definition: ROCKFISH is a common term for several species of fish, referring to their tendency to hide among rocks.

entries.label: alaska pollock
entries.definition: The Alaska pollock (Gadus chalcogrammus) is a marine fish species of the cod family Gadidae.

entries.label: European anchovy
entries.definition: The European anchovy (Engraulis encrasicolus) is a forage fish somewhat related to the herring.

entries.label: mahi-mahi
entries.definition: Mahi-mahi is a species of fish, it's sometimes called "dolphinfish," but it's unrelated to dolphins. It's a large, colorful saltwater fish found in warm and temperate waters around the world, known for its firm, lean, mildly sweet white-to-pinkish flesh. Flavor and texture: Mild, slightly sweet flavor with a firm, meaty texture — often compared to swordfish or tuna, but lighter and less oily.

entries.label: milkfish
entries.definition: Milkfish (Chanos chanos) is a mild-flavored, silvery fish that's a staple food in parts of Southeast Asia, especially the Philippines, Indonesia, and Taiwan. Texture and flavor: The flesh is soft, slightly fatty, and has a mild taste that takes on marinades and seasonings well. It's notoriously bony, with many small, fine bones running through the flesh. This has led to specialty products like "bo

entries.label: monkfish
entries.definition: "Anglerfish" is a broad term for an order of fish (Lophiiformes) known for using a fleshy growth on their head like a fishing lure to attract prey. The fish sold as "monkfish" in seafood markets typically refers to species in the genus Lophius — like the American anglerfish (Lophius americanus) or European anglerfish (Lophius piscatorius) — which live on the seafloor in relatively shallow coastal

entries.label: loup
entries.definition: Loup est un nom vernaculaire ambigu désignant en français certains poissons prédateurs marins.

entries.label: Atlantic wolffish
entries.definition: The Atlantic wolffish (Anarhichas lupus), also known as the seawolf, Atlantic catfish, ocean catfish, devil fish, wolf eel (the common name for its Pacific relative), woof or sea cat, is a marine fish of the wolffish family Anarhichadidae.

entries.label: blue whiting
entries.definition: The blue whiting, Micromesistius poutassou, one of the two species in the genus Micromesistius in the cod family, is common in the northeast Atlantic Ocean from Morocco to Iceland and Spitsbergen

entries.label: bluefish
entries.definition: Bluefish (Pomatomus saltatrix) is a species of saltwater fish commonly eaten as food, especially along the Atlantic coasts of the US, and also found in various other parts of the world. Flavor and texture: It has a stronger, more "fishy" flavor than mild white fish like cod or tilapia. The flesh is oily/fatty (similar in that regard to mackerel or salmon), which gives it a rich taste but also mean

entries.label: burbot
entries.definition: Burbot (Lota lota) is a freshwater fish — and actually the only member of the cod family (Gadidae) that lives entirely in fresh water rather than the ocean. It's edible and considered quite good eating — sometimes nicknamed "poor man's lobster" because its liver and flesh are prized by some anglers, especially for winter ice-fishing.

entries.label: butterfish
entries.definition: Butterfish is the common name for a couple of different fish species, most notably: Escolar (Lepidocybium flavobrunneum) — sometimes marketed as "butterfish," this deep-sea fish has an extremely high oil content that gives it a rich, buttery texture and mouthfeel, hence the name. It's popular in sushi restaurants (sometimes mislabeled as "white tuna"); American butterfish (Peprilus triacanthus) —

entries.label: American butterfish
entries.definition: American butterfish (Peprilus triacanthus) is a small, deep-bodied fish from the northwest Atlantic, ranging from Labrador down to Florida's Gulf coast. Flavor and texture: It has soft, delicate, oily flesh with a mild, sweet flavor — the "butter" in the name comes from that rich, tender texture rather than any actual buttery taste. The flesh is white and flakes easily when cooked.

entries.label: capelin
entries.definition: The capelin or caplin (Mallotus villosus) is a small forage fish of the smelt family found in the North Atlantic, North Pacific, and Arctic oceans. Commercialement, le capelan est utilisé comme produit alimentaire, et dans l'industrie des huiles de poisson. Sa chair a un goût agréable, ressemblant à celle du hareng. Les œufs de capelan ("masago") sont des produits alimentaires coûteux.

entries.label: carp
entries.definition: Carp is a freshwater fish that's been eaten by humans for thousands of years — it's actually one of the oldest farmed food fish in the world, with cultivation going back to ancient China. Taste and texture: Mild, slightly sweet, and somewhat earthy or "muddy" tasting, especially if it comes from murky water. Farm-raised carp raised in cleaner water tends to taste better. The flesh is firm but has

entries.label: cisco
entries.definition: Cisco is a freshwater whitefish in the genus Coregonus, found mainly in the Great Lakes and other cold lakes across North America (and some in Europe/Asia too). It's related to salmon and trout. Cisco  has a mild, delicate flavor — similar to other whitefish, slightly sweet. The texture is tender, flaky, fine-textured flesh — fairly delicate, can fall apart easily if overcooked.

entries.label: cusk
entries.definition: Cusk (Brosme brosme) is a bottom-dwelling fish in the cod family (Gadidae), found in the cold waters of the North Atlantic — off the coasts of New England, Atlantic Canada, and northern Europe. Cusk has firm, white flesh similar to cod or haddock, and is prized by some for its mild flavor. It's often sold fresh or used in chowders.

entries.label: nile perch
entries.definition: The Nile perch (Lates niloticus), also known as the African snook, Goliath perch, Giant lates or the Victoria perch, is a species of freshwater fish in family Latidae of order Perciformes. It is widespread throughout much of the Afrotropical realm.

entries.label: European perch
entries.definition: The European perch (Perca fluviatilis), also known as the common perch, redfin perch, big-scaled redfin, English perch, Eurasian perch, Eurasian river perch, Hatch or in Anglophone parts of Europe, simply the perch, is a predatory species of the freshwater perch native to Europe and northern Asia.

entries.label: European seabass
entries.definition: The European bass (Dicentrarchus labrax) is a primarily ocean-going fish native to the waters off Europe's western and southern and Africa's northern coasts.

entries.label: striped bass
entries.definition: The striped bass (Morone saxatilis), also called the Atlantic striped bass, striper, linesider, rock or rockfish, is an anadromous perciform fish of the family Moronidae found primarily along the Atlantic coast of North America.

entries.label: European plaice
entries.definition: The European plaice (Pleuronectes platessa) is a commercially important flatfish

entries.definition: The common sole, Dover sole, or black sole (Solea solea) is a species of flatfish in the family Soleidae.It is a largest fish in solea (fish) genus. Chefs prize Dover sole for its mild, buttery, sweet flavour and versatility, and for its ease of filleting.

Very high in omega-3 fatty acids, even more than salmon per serving

entries.label: scup
entries.definition: Scup is a small saltwater fish found along the Atlantic coast of North America, from Nova Scotia down to Florida, though it's most abundant from Cape Cod to Cape Hatteras. Flavor and texture: Mild, slightly sweet white flesh, similar in character to other porgies or small snappers. It's a lean fish.

entries.label: spot
entries.definition: A small saltwater fish common along the U.S. Atlantic and Gulf coasts. Spot has mild, sweet, flaky white flesh. It's popular in Southern U.S. cooking — often pan-fried or deep-fried whole (scaled and gutted), since the bones are easy to work around once cooked. It's a favorite at fish fries in the Carolinas, Georgia, and along the Gulf Coast.

entries.label: tilapia
entries.definition: Tilapia is one of the most widely farmed and eaten fish in the world — a mild, freshwater (or brackish-water) fish that's become a staple in supermarkets and restaurants globally. entries.label: tilefish
entries.definition: Tilefish is a type of saltwater fish found mainly in the western Atlantic Ocean, from the northeastern U.S. down through the Gulf of Mexico. There are a few species, but the most commonly eaten ones are golden tilefish (also called "white tilefish" in markets) and blueline tilefish. entries.label: tuna
entries.definition: A tuna is a saltwater fish that belongs to the tribe Thunnini, a subgrouping of the Scombridae family.

entries.label: albacore
entries.definition: The albacore (Thunnus alalunga), known also as the longfin tuna, is a species of tuna of the order Perciformes.

entries.label: yellowfin tuna

entries.label: common ling
entries.definition: This is a long, eel-like fish in the cod family (Gadidae), found in the North Atlantic, particularly around European and North American coasts. It has: A firm, white, flaky flesh similar to cod or haddock; A mild, slightly sweet flavor;A long, slender body (can grow quite large, sometimes over a meter)

entries.label: blue ling
entries.definition: Blue ling lives in much deeper water than common ling. The flesh is white, firm, and mild — used in much the same way as common ling or cod, though it's less commonly sold fresh to consumers and more often ends up in processed or filleted products.

entries.label: lingcod
entries.definition: Lingcod is a type of fish popular on the West Coast of the US, it's not actually a cod. It's related to greenlings. Flavor and texture: Mild, slightly sweet white fish with a firm, flaky texture. Often compared to halibut or cod but a bit more delicate.

entries.label: mackerel
entries.definition: Mackerel is an oily fish, popular in cuisines around the world for its rich flavor and nutritional value. It is a general name for several related species of fast-swimming, saltwater fish (like Atlantic mackerel, king mackerel, and Spanish mackerel). entries.label: wheat vermicelli
entries.definition: Vermicelli (seviyan) is a thin, thread-like noodle made by extruding wheat dough — typically from refined flour or semolina — through fine dies, then drying (and often lightly roasting). Popular across South Asia and the Middle East, it has a mild, neutral-to-toasty taste depending on roasting, with a delicate, springy texture once cooked. entries.label: tortilla
entries.definition: A tortilla is a type of thin flatbread, typically made from nixtamalized corn or wheat flour.

entries.label: cake
entries.definition: CAKE is a form of sweet food that is usually baked. The most commonly used cake ingredients include flour, sugar, eggs, butter or oil or margarine, a liquid, and leavening agents, such as baking soda or baking powder.

entries.label: Petit-Beurre
entries.definition: The "PETIT BEURRE", or "Véritable Petit Beurre", also known under the initials "VPB", is a kind of shortbread from Nantes, that is best known in France. It is the Petit Beurre of the LU society, which has become a success worldwide.

entries.label: crouton
entries.definition: A CROUTON is a piece of sautéed or rebaked bread, often cubed and seasoned, that is used to add texture and flavor to salads as an accompaniment to soups and stews, or eaten as a snack food.

entries.label: tofu
entries.definition: TOFU is a food prepared by coagulating soy milk and then pressing the resulting curds into solid white blocks of varying softness. Tofu has very little flavor or smell of its own. Consequently, tofu can be used in both savory or sweet dishes, acting as a bland background for presenting the flavors of the other ingredients used. In order to flavor the tofu it is often marinated in soy sauce, chilli

entries.label: marzipan
entries.definition: MARZIPAN is a confection consisting primarily of sugar or honey and almond meal (ground almonds), sometimes augmented with almond oil or extract.

entries.label: soy milk
entries.definition: SOY MILK or soymilk is a plant-based drink produced by soaking and grinding soybeans, boiling the mixture, and filtering out remaining particulates.

entries.label: omelette
entries.definition: In cuisine, an OMELETTE is a dish made from beaten eggs fried with butter or oil in a frying pan (without stirring as in scrambled egg). It is quite common for the omelette to be folded around a filling such as cheese, chives, vegetables, mushrooms, meat (often ham or bacon), or some combination of the above. entries.definition: CHORIZO or chouriço is a type of pork sausage. In Europe, chorizo is a fermented, cured, smoked sausage, which may be sliced and eaten without cooking, or added as an ingredient to add flavor to other dishes. entries.label: ice cream
entries.definition: ICE CREAM is a sweetened frozen food typically eaten as a snack or dessert. It may be made from dairy milk or cream, or soy, cashew, coconut or almondmilk, and is flavored with a sweetener, either sugar or an alternative, and any spice, such as cocoa or vanilla. Colourings are usually added, in addition to stabilizers.

entries.label: vanilla ice cream
entries.definition: VANILLA ICE CREAM is flavored by artificial or natural vanilla flavoring. The type of vanilla used to flavor ice cream varies by location.

entries.label: harissa
entries.definition: HARISSA is a Tunisian hot chili pepper paste, the main ingredients of which are roasted red peppers, Baklouti pepper, serrano peppers, and other hot chili peppers, spices and herbs such as garlic paste, coriander seed, saffron, rose, or caraway, as well as some vegetable or olive oil to carry the oil-soluble flavors.

entries.label: ketchup
entries.definition: KETCHUP is a sauce used as a condiment. Ketchup is a sweet and tangy sauce now typically made from tomatoes, sugar, and vinegar, with assorted seasonings and spices. The specific spices and flavors vary, but commonly include onions, allspice, coriander, cloves, cumin, garlic, and mustard; and sometimes include celery, cinnamon or ginger.

entries.label: marinade
entries.definition: Marination is the process of soaking foods in a seasoned, often acidic, liquid (MARINADE) before cooking.

entries.label: mayonnaise
entries.definition: MAYONNAISE, informally mayo, is a thick cold sauce or dressing usually used in sandwiches and composed salads or on chips. It is a stable emulsion of oil, egg yolk, and acid, either vinegar or lemon juice.

entries.label: soy sauce

entries.label: worcestershire sauce
entries.definition: WORCESTERSHIRE SAUCE is a fermented liquid condiment created in the city of Worcester. Worcestershire sauce is frequently used to enhance food and drink recipes.

entries.label: bolognese sauce
entries.definition: BOLOGNESE SAUCE is a meat-based sauce in Italian cuisine. It is customarily used to dress tagliatelle al ragù and to prepare lasagne alla bolognese.

entries.label: cream sauce

entries.label: sambal

entries.label: sambal oelek

entries.label: béarnaise sauce

entries.label: pesto
entries.definition: PESTO is a sauce originating in Genoa, Italy. It traditionally consists of crushed garlic, European pine nuts, coarse salt, basil leaves, hard cheese, all blended with olive oil.

entries.definition: ISOMALT is a sugar substitute, a type of sugar alcohol used primarily for its sugar-like physical properties. It has little to no impact on blood sugar levels, and does not stimulate the release of insulin. Isomalt is widely used for the production of sugar-free candy, especially hard-boiled candy.

entries.label: E965
entries.definition: MALTITOL is a sugar alcohol (a polyol) used as a sugar substitute. It has 75–90% of the sweetness of sucrose (table sugar) and nearly identical properties, except for browning. Maltitol's high sweetness allows it to be used without being mixed with other sweeteners. It is used in candy manufacture, particularly sugar-free hard candy, chewing gum, chocolates, baked goods, and ice cream.

entries.label: E1104
entries.definition: A LIPASE is any enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of fats (lipids). Lipases serve important roles in human practices as ancient as yogurt and cheese fermentation. Lipases are generally animal sourced, but can also be sourced microbially.
